subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY PRIME MINISTER ON APRIL 27.
MR. ARGUE    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY PRIME MINISTER ON APRIL 27.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on Wednesday, April 27, at a time, sir, when I was not in the house or I would have answered it at that time. The Prime Minister had this to say, as reported at page 3335 of Hansard:
When about two weeks ago I spoke on this subject and referred to the possibility of there being a debate, my natural view was that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), having regard to Monday being the last private members' day, would have permitted the clearing away of a number of cases on a subject that is receiving general attention from members of the C.C.F. party.
I want to make it perfectly clear that this suggestion was not made to me nor, as far as
I know, to any other member of the C.C.F. party. On the basis of our attitude on this question in the past, on the basis of proposals we have made about bringing on such a debate, I would suggest that any proposal for unanimous consent to have the subject of apartheid brought forward on Monday would have received our consent. The Prime Minister went on to say:
If that had been so, we could have placed on private members' motions a motion similar to the one indicated by the hon. gentleman-
That is, the Leader of the Opposition.
-and with consent could have proceeded to discuss it.
I want to point out that if such a private member's motion, not a government motion, had been placed on the order paper it would have been No. 53 and could not have been debated at that point except by unanimous consent. My question of privilege is that I was not asked on behalf of the C.C.F. group to agree to any alteration of business, and I would point out that anything that could have been done by consent on Monday could have been done by consent on Wednesday.

speechtext:

For a copy of all correspondence, telegrams and other documents exchanged between the federal government or any agency or branch thereof, and any provincial government, person, or organization

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA PENITENTIARY INMATES

spoke to the hon. gentleman about this motion, and I think I should point out to the house that the subject matter dealt with therein, amnesty, pardon, parole or remission, it seems to me is one dealing with the prerogative powers of the crown, with the exercise of which the government is specifically charged, and as such it has always been a principle of this house that such a matter should not be inquired into by the house and that the documents relating thereto should be treated as confidential. subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA PENITENTIARY INMATES

For a copy of all correspondence, telegrams and other documents exchanged, during the past twelve months, between the federal government, or any agency or branch thereof, and the province of Newfoundland; and any interdepartmental correspondence and documents, dealing with disallowance or otherwise of labour legislation passed by the legislature of Newfoundland.

Since that time the hon. member and I have bad a discussion, and he pointed out that what he really had in mind in the words "interdepartmental correspondence" was a copy of any order in council or similar document dealing officially with the matter of disallowance.
He also pointed out that previously there had been a number of occasions when such

documents of the class I have just mentioned were produced. On that basis, if the words "interdepartmental correspondence", were to be interpreted as meaning the official report of cabinet decisions regarding disallowance, I would have no objection.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO PREVENT CLOSING OF MINES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. Can the minister give an assurance to the house that the government is taking the necessary action to avert the closing of coal mines in Nova Scotia this year, as contemplated by certain coal operators of the area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Comfois (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO PREVENT CLOSING OF MINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answering this question I think it would be well to inform the house that around April 20 last, we were notified by Mr. A. L. Fairley, Jr., president of Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, Limited, that seven of their nine collieries would not be in production for five days commencing Monday, April 25. This is the first of a series of temporary shut-downs that will be scheduled during the summer months of this year. They are caused by a shrinkage in coal consuming markets due to competition from secondary power, natural gas and oil. It is not possible at this time to state the total number of non-producing days that will be in effect this year.
The total production of the seven collieries for a five day period would average approximately 85,000 tons. The two collieries which will continue in full-time operation are No. 26, Dominion Coal Company at Glace Bay, Cape Breton Island and McBean, Acadia Coal Company at Thorburn, Nova Scotia mainland.
At the same time I should say that last week the fact-finding committee held a sitting here in Ottawa attended by the Minister of National Revenue and myself, Premier Stanfield, representatives of the united mine workers association and the provincial minister of mines, Mr. Manson and also the chairman of the coal board. They have produced their report and conclusions based on the hearings they held, and we are actively studying those conclusions and recommendations. Everything is now before the government, and when I have a statement to make I will inform the house.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO PREVENT CLOSING OF MINES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister inform the house whether any action has been taken not only to prevent a cut-back but to avert the complete closing of certain mines?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO PREVENT CLOSING OF MINES
speechtext: I should say, Mr. Speaker, that there were no closings at all during the whole winter. The only thing that is contemplated at this time by the company is a temporary shut-down during the summer months. As far as complete closings are concerned, no decision has been taken, even by the company.

Mr. Speaker, there are a good many subjects on which the opposition might, with profit to the Canadian people, express grievances against the administration of the country by the present incumbents of the treasury benches; but we have felt that it would be indelicate at this particular time, with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) absent from the country on the nation's business, to introduce a motion which would be in any way controversial. Therefore I have been chosen, for obvious reasons, to introduce a motion- which I intend to do before I resume my seat but not immediately-which we believe will commend itself to every hon. member; which will not express any condemnation whatsoever of the present administration, but will instead make an appeal to the administration to undertake certain things which we believe, and which we feel some of their supporters will also believe, would be in the general interests of Canada.
This, of course, is not an unprecedented use of the right of the opposition on a supply motion. The Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Fleming) will, I know, well recall several occasions on which this course was followed when he was over here and the opposition invited the government and its supporters, perhaps its supporters more particularly, to join in a unanimous expression of the views of the house. I do hope that when the vote comes tomorrow it will be possible to have the somewhat rare spectacle on supply days of such a unanimous vote.
2.	1960
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces
What I am going to talk about is the present position of the Atlantic provinces. This will not surprise the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) or the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) or the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) or the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Browne), all of whom are here today. We can only commend them for being here, unlike some of their colleagues on some previous occasions, and for anticipating that such a course would be followed. I said that I thought the government would perhaps be more apt to listen to this kind of appeal at this particular time. I do not propose to elaborate on that statement. I think it will be understood by every hon. member who wishes to understand and not misunderstand me.
It is just three years since the people of this country were engaged in listening to the candidates in an election campaign which some of us on both sides of the house are not apt to forget for a considerable time. In the Atlantic provinces the people were told by some hon. gentlemen now opposite that they were going to do something in the Atlantic provinces to increase the economic activity of that area, to increase the welfare of people in that area, to give it a closer approach to equality with other parts of the country than had been the case during what they were pleased to describe as the 22 years of Liberal neglect.
I want to say a word or two very briefly about those 22 years of so-called Liberal neglect in the Atlantic provinces. First of all I should like to recall to the minds of hon. members one of the best of all indices by which one can judge the effects of that neglect. Hon. members will recall that during the war it was necessary for the government of Canada to enter into agreements with the pro-vinical governments-with all of them, I might add, because all of them did enter into these agreements at that time-for the renting of the direct tax fields, income and corporation taxes, that were occupied at that time by the federal government and by most of the provinces, though not by all of them.
In the year 1945, at the end of the war, the Atlantic provinces were receiving by way of rental payments-I should rather say the maritime provinces, because at that time Newfoundland was not a part of Canada-* $7J million in lieu of the exercise by those governments of their taxing powers in those fields. That was in 1945. In the year 1956-57, the last full year the Liberals were in office, as the Minister of Finance is so fond of describing it, the three maritime provinces- here I am deliberately leaving Newfoundland out so the comparison will be exact-were

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces receiving $43 million from the same taxation fields in lieu of the exercise of their rights of taxation, that is to say, about five and a half times as much as they had been receiving in 1945. In 1957-58, the year in which this government came into office, without any thanks whatever to this government because, as the Minister of Finance pointed out the other day, he voted against this legislation about which I am talking, the three maritime provinces were receiving under the taxsharing arrangements $52 million. The increase made by Mr. Harris' legislation of 1956, which came into operation in the year 1957-58, was $9 million, and this was in the last year of our so-called neglect.
What does this mean, sir? It means that in only the last 12 years out of the 22 years what these provinces were receiving in the way of tax-sharing payments or equalization payments had risen from $7.75 million to $52 million or had been multiplied, as hon. members can very well see, something like seven times. Now, that is a very considerable increase indeed.
If other evidence were needed or desired as to the way the maritime provinces fared during this period that has been described as a period of Liberal neglect, there are two or three rather striking statistics that I can cite. In the first place, between 1936 and 1956 the population of greater Halifax rose from about 75,000 to 165,000. The number of motor vehicles registered in the province of Nova Scotia rose in that period from 45,000 to 150,000. The provincial revenues of Nova Scotia rose from $10 million to $57 million. This does not suggest, sir, that there was no advance in that area. In New Brunswick the population increased even faster than it did in Nova Scotia. The population of the whole province rose from 428,000 to 565,000 during those 20 Liberal years. The number of motor vehicles in New Brunswick rose from 31,000 to 116,000. I do not say that the motor vehicle is the only measure of the wealth of a community, but it is certainly a measure and perhaps, in our kind of society, not an altogether inaccurate measure.
I have had some calculations made and to the best of my ability I have based those, so far as possible, to take account of the fact that a certain thing did not appear at the end of a calendar year or at the end of a fiscal year. A certain very important event, for instance, happened on June 21, 1957, and this makes it a little difficult to measure these things precisely. However, it does appear that during the three years Mr. Harris was minister of finance of this country the personal income, the real income-here I am making due allowance for the change in the value of


money and for inflation so the figures will be comparable-of the people in the Atlantic provinces increased at a very much more rapid rate than has been the case since. There has been some increase since, but the increase during the last three years the Liberals were in office was very much more marked.
When one turns to employment, the situation is even more startling. I am not saying anything about whether or not these figures are an accurate measure of unemployment; that is another matter. But certainly if you take the figures for one year and compare them with another year they are a pretty accurate measure of the change. When we were appealing to the people in the spring of 1957, or at the available date closest to that for purposes of comparison, and this is the poorest date I could take from our point of view, there were registered at the unemployment offices and looking for work in the Atlantic provinces, nearly 95,000 persons. On March 20, 1958 there were 135,000 and on March 19, 1959 116,800. This year there were 116,500. When you make allowance, sir, for the fact that in the last year the fishermen were treated as though they did not exist and' were deducted from the figures, it will be seen that unemployment is very much more considerable in the Atlantic region now than it was when we went to the country.
Are these figures for the four provinces?

Yes, for what is called the Atlantic region. I must point out, of course, that when we went to the country in 1957 there was a considerable amount of seasonal unemployment and had been during that past winter, as everybody on the Liberal side of the house admitted. In contrast, we have been told by the Minister of Labour and by other hon. gentlemen opposite that the recession is now over; that we are at the beginning of a year in which they expect a very substantial improvement, if not a boom.
When you look at certain of the key industries in the Atlantic area you can once more make a comparison which is not very flattering. A few moments ago the hon. member for Gloucester asked the minister of mines a question about coal. Of course we remember the advertisements, and we remember those pictures that appeared in the newspapers of Mr. Diefenbaker and Mr. Stanfield side by side on the public platform in Nova Scotia during the June election campaign of 1957, promising to increase coal production. Our leader during that election campaign told the truth. He said he would not promise to increase coal production, but he would

promise that we would not allow the coal towns to become ghost towns. He was pilloried by hon. gentlemen opposite all over the maritime provinces for that truthful, straightforward statement. I think today, when you compare the two of them, you would rather have been responsible for making the one statement than the other, because coal production has declined steadily ever since that statement was made.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
At that time did not his leader, Mr. St. Laurent, suggest that coal was too valuable to be burned and should be kept in the ground?

I am very grateful, as I always am, to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), who has just asked me a question. He has given me an opportunity to state what Mr. St. Laurent said. I was there and I heard what he said. I have in my files the text of what he stated, although I have not got it right here. I will not guarantee to reproduce every word, but I will guarantee to give the correct sense of what he said. What he said was this. He believed that the time would come before too many years when coal, as a chemical and as a source of other chemicals, would be much more valuable than it would be as a fuel, and that apart from any other consideration he believed that was one reason why it would not be desirable to increase the production of coal. But he went on to say and to make very clear that what we intended to do-as we had been doing, I might say, up to that time-was to see that the coal industry was not allowed to decline to the point where these towns would become ghost towns. That was our position, and it was honestly stated.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

Is the hon. member now saying that the Fredericton Gleaner incorrectly reported what Mr. St. Laurent said at that time, or is he now prepared to make an apology as called for in the front page editorial?

There is a certain non sequitur in the hon. member's question which I shall deal with a moment. I believe the Fredericton Gleaner reported quite accurately what Mr. St. Laurent said, but I also believe that it misinterpreted what he said. About that particular matter I have no
2, 1960	3453
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces apology of any kind to make. I am sorry- and the hon. member knows this as well as I do-that I have not been able to find that particular copy of the Fredericton Gleaner. I have really made a thorough search. I even went to the length of asking the hon. gentleman to lend me his copy so I could refresh my memory as to precisely what it said.
I will see that it is made available.

I shall be glad at any time to deal in detail with the point. But after all, whether I apologize or do not apologize to the Fredericton Gleaner is not going to change the fate of this country very much. I do not think the hon. gentleman and I want to get into any controversy just now about this matter. However, if I said anything that was inaccurate, I think hon. members know well enough that I have always been willing to admit an inaccuracy and correct it whenever it was drawn to my attention. I hope I shall always continue to do that. Whenever I find one myself, as hon. members will recall from certain experience in this house, I have not hesitated to do that either.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that it seems to me the time has clearly now arrived when we cannot go on contemplating much longer this steady decline in the coal industry without doing two things. The first is to try to arrest that decline to the limit that it is possible to do it, using every reasonable device; but also certain other devices should be used for putting something else in its place in that area, something which I think is perhaps even more important.
The situation in the fisheries is not as serious as it is in the coal industry, but it is serious. The output of the Atlantic fisheries is nearly all sold outside of Canada. The fisheries industry is, to a much more substantial degree even than the wheat industry, dependent upon export markets. I think that fact is not nearly as widely realized in Canada as it should be. Like all our primary export industries the fishing industry has suffered in the last few years from the cost-price squeeze. The price of the product has not gone up or has not gone up substantially in most cases-in some cases has not gone up at all and in some cases has gone down -while the cost of production has gone up and the cost of living of the producers has also gone up. You can make almost a complete parallel between the cod fishery and the wheat industry from an economic standpoint, except in one respect. While the government once in a while, seems to be aware

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces of the wheat industry-although they are less and less aware of it as time goes on-they seem to be totally unaware of the plight of the fishermen.
Agriculture in the Atlantic provinces is unquestionably very much worse off than it was three years ago. Perhaps relatively it is not much worse off than is agriculture in the rest of Canada which, after the false dawn, has been overcast by the clouds emanating from the government rain-making machine so far as the farmers' hopes are concerned. Farmers often hope for rain at the right time but unfortunately the rain from this government always seems to come at the wrong time, namely at the time when the crops are ready for harvesting and not at the time when the crops would be improved.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I had better drop that figure of speech before it drops me. However, there are among my colleagues from the Atlantic provinces others who have a much more intimate knowledge of this subject than I. It is true that I have in my constituency two of the best agricultural areas in the whole of Newfoundland, but even when I have said that I could be accused of exaggerating if I said that agriculture had the same importance in Newfoundland that it has in any of the three other maritime provinces, because up to now it has not had the same importance.
What about provincial finances? I say something about this because, as I said, I am seeking to be absolutely fair about this whole matter. I say there is no question but that in one or two respects the governments of the Atlantic provinces are better off than they would have been if no change had been made in the law since June 21, 1957. I at once admit that fact. I have never failed to admit it in any circumstances. I think the adoption by this parliament, at the request of the present government, of the Atlantic provinces grants was a beneficent measure which I was pleased to support and for which I have always given this government credit.
I think we must also give this government credit-and perhaps they will not be so anxious to take this credit as the one I have just given them-for the fact that when Mr. Harris was minister of finance it was possible for all the Atlantic provinces to float loans in Canada at rates of interest which were considerably below those which have been prevailing in the last year or so. What is more, Mr. Harris was paying off the national debt. In the last year he was in office he paid off a billion dollars of the national debt, a fact which left a great deal of room for other public borrowers to go to the market. In his day the provincial governments were not [Mr. Pickersgill.l
facing from the national treasury or from the minister of finance the kind of competition which they have faced in the last year and which has driven them to borrow in New York, with consequences which it is not easy to foresee but which could be quite serious.
As to these Atlantic provinces grants- and I say this because I anticipate that the matter will be raised by some hon. gentleman opposite-I want to say a word or two about their earlier history. The idea of something more than tax rental or equalization was first proposed by Mr. Henry Hicks when he was premier of Nova Scotia, at the preliminary meeting of the federal-provincial conference of 1955, on April 26 of that year. The proposal will be found set out at pages 22, 23 and 24 of the proceedings. I do not intend to say anything beyond drawing attention to the fact that it was made in terms which were of universal application to every province of Canada. What Mr. Hicks suggested was really carrying out the idea of fiscal need as set out in the Rowell-Sirois report and providing a formula to meet somewhat different conditions.
In the autumn, at the main conference on October 3, 1955 Mr. Hicks elaborated his proposal and Mr. Flemming, the premier of New Brunswick, also made a proposal which was somewhat different in character. At that particular time those proposals were very seriously considered by the government of the day; I say that of my own knowledge. The government of the day had already in its proposals to that conference suggested making another $100 million a year available to the provinces under the new legislation, over and above the old. It was a little over $100 million. Hon. members will see that by looking at Hansard for last Wednesday, when the Minister of Finance replied to a starred question of mine and indicated that in the last full year the Liberals were in office the provinces received or were given abatements equal to $523.3 million, and in the next year, 1957-58, these payments and abatements amounted to $628.9 million, that is to say an increase of nearly $106 million. Then I asked if any part of that increase was the result of legislation passed since June 21, 1957 and the answer was no.
Therefore the whole of that $100 million increase, which I may say parenthetically, and only parenthetically, hon. gentlemen opposite from the Prime Minister down constantly claim in their speeches as something done by the present government, was in fact entirely the result of legislation which the Minister of Finance told us, in a candid moment the other day in the house, he voted against and opposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right, because of its inadequacy.
That is not at all what the hon. gentleman said at that time. The hon. gentleman said that the scheme was too complicated for him to understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.
It was true then and I am not sure it is not true still.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not true now and never was true.
Well, the hon. gentleman can tell us the truth when he gets up to make a three-hour speech a little later in the debate.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Yes.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us on what page the budget of Mr. Harris shows this amount under the Atlantic adjustment grant; in what year and in what section of the budget?

I am not sure I understand the hon. gentleman's question, and I suspect that he did not hear what I said. I said that we were not able to accede to the request of Mr. Hicks, and we did not accede to it for this reason. I was quite candid about this; it is well known because, after all, it is part of history, and I am not revealing any great secret when I say this. The reason was that we had already offered to increase the payments to the provinces out of the national treasury by $100 million. In other words we were going to reduce the amount of income tax and corporation tax which would go into the federal treasury and put it into the provincial treasuries to the extent of $100 million, which we thought at that time was a very substantial increase indeed. It was an increase from a little over $500 million to a little over $600 million, in other words an increase of 20 per cent. We simply did not believe that at that time, having regard to all the other demands on the treasury, we would be justified in reducing the amount in the federal treasury by a still greater amount because that would have affected the balance [DOT]of ways and means.
That was the position we took. Whether we were right or wrong, it was the position we took. I have always said that, notwithstanding the fact that we took that position, I would give credit to this government for taking a different position and for accepting Mr. Hicks' suggestion which we did not accept. I do not think I can make it any plainer than that; we did not accept it but this government has accepted it.
2. 1960
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces
However, they did accept it with one modification, which I must say I do not think was an improvement. Mr. Hicks himself said this in the legislature; it has been said by me in this hosue before, and I say it again. My own opinion is that the position of the Atlantic provinces would be stronger if these Atlantic provinces grants were not called Atlantic provinces grants and if the formula was applicable to all the provinces if they found themselves in a similar position.
Now, if I understand the formula aright there is no other province at the present time which would find itself in that position, and we would hope there never would be. But there was a time during the thirties when Saskatchewan, and to some extent Manitoba and Alberta, were in just as bad a position as any of the maritime provinces. We do not believe that will ever happen again; but after all the taxpayers all over Canada pay the taxes which go into making these payments, and we should not forget them. I believe that if the government had gone the whole of the way Mr. Hicks suggested and had adopted a formula which, while in fact it would only have provided funds for the Atlantic provinces, would have been applicable in like circumstances right across the country, that would have been a better way of doing it. It would have accomplished the purpose just as well, and it would have created a better impression. I may say that this view was also taken at the conference in 1957 by Mr. Douglas Campbell of Manitoba and by Mr. T. C. Douglas of Saskatchewan, and I am not sure that it was not taken by some of the other premiers. I happen to remember because I went as a spectator at that conference, and I heard them take that position.

There is another thing I want to say about the Atlantic provinces grants before I leave the subject. When they were brought forward by the Minister of Finance in this house in January of 1958 they were described by Mr. Kirk, then the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, as deficiency payments and that is, of course, precisely what they are. They are payments made because the income and the taxable capacity of these provinces is below the national average, and substantially below it.
How did that happen with you in office?

I am pleased to answer that question of the hon. member. If you had gone back to 1935 and compared their position then with that of some other parts of Canada you would have found that there was a vast improvement in the period we were in office. I can tell hon. members that there are lots of people in the Atlantic provinces somewhat older than the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) who are old enough to remember that.
Do you remember?

But I am afraid that if we are not careful this may-in the words of a distinguished friend of mine-degenerate into a debate.
These deficiency payments are needed and there is no one who would question that in the light of the experience of the three years. I do not believe that any government even if it wanted to would dare to terminate these arrangements. But I do say that what we really want to do, what should be the aim of all of us and what I really believe is our aim -although perhaps some of us have a better aim than others-is to end the deficiency so that the payments will not be needed to correct a basic weakness in the economy of the Atlantic provinces.
How is that going to be done? That is the problem. I have already alluded to the weak position of agriculture, to the coal industry
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces and its serious plight, to the relative and absolute decline in the fisheries. About all these things I believe a good deal could be and should be done and on various other occasions suggestions have been made. If some of the suggestions, for example, made in another debate the other day by my friend the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Granger) were carried out they would be a step in that direction.
Even if the fisheries were restored, even if the coal industry employed as many people today as it did in 1956, even if agriculture was on a much sounder foundation than it is at present, with the population and the number of young people there are today in the Atlantic provinces those industries could not possibly provide the employment that is needed in that area in order to have a healthy expanding economy.
What about the other industries? There are some healthy industries. On the whole the forest industries are in a very healthy condition. They have their ups and downs from year to year, but happily this is one industry that gives signs of having a somewhat better year than last year; at least that is true of some parts of the forest industry. If this matter is quiescent for the moment, sir, I would go on to say that there is no doubt in my mind-making the very big assumption that was made by the Gordon commission and that in discussing any domestic issue we always have to make-if there is going to be any future and we are not going to face a nuclear war, about which, of course, others are more competent to speak than I am; but assuming that there is going to be a future, I do not think there can be any doubt that one would predict that the future of the forest industries of the Atlantic provinces is probably better than others in the long term, because happily the forest is a continuing crop and happily in the main it is being well cropped. I am sure there is room for some improvement there, too, as there always will be, but great steps have -been taken in all the provinces to see that this most valuable of all the crops in the Atlantic provinces is maintained as a continuing crop.
There is no doubt there will be some expansion of the industry but the area of the provinces is not going to be expanded. The accessibility of the forests may be somewhat improved, as it is being improved by the spread of roads, particularly in Newfoundland, where it has been so marked in the last few years. But this is not the whole answer. This industry may, with increased fabrication, provide a somewhat expanded employment, and particularly perhaps in Newfoundland which is at an earlier stage of development than the other provinces.
The mining industry, of course, apart from coal mining, is happily showing signs of improvement. I see the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) smiling and about this he can smile. This is particularly true of the iron mines of the Labrador, and I am sure the minister will be the first to admit, that they are expanding even more rapidly in Newfoundland than they are in his province. There is no doubt that one of the biggest sources of immediately increased employment will be the development of the iron mines of the Carol lake and the Wabush lake areas, and all the development ancillary thereto.


Undoubtedly, too, as the demand for power becomes greater and the possibility of its economic exploitation becomes more real, the development of the vast hydro electric resources of the Hamilton river will also give a stimulus, I would hope, not only to the province of Newfoundland but also that all the surplus power would not be sent westward into Quebec and Ontario, but that some of it would go eastward and in a southerly direction to supplement the less extensive power resources of the other Atlantic provinces and that technical advances would be such in the next few years as to make that possible.
One of the industries which I believe will expand the most in the next few years is the tourist industry. I believe we are not doing nearly enough to accelerate that expansion which is one direction in which we could move more quickly and get immediate results; but, when all is said and done, sir, if we are to have a development at all comparable with that of the rest of Canada there must in addition be the development of secondary industries in the Atlantic provinces, not on the scale of Ontario and Quebec-I do not think anyone would expect that-but on a very much greater scale than exists at the present time.
This area is dependent, far more than the Canadian average on trade. If between one quarter and one third of our population is dependent on trade for their incomes, it must be over half in the Atlantic provinces and far more than half in the province of Newfoundland. That is why it is very hard even for Tories in the Atlantic provinces to be protectionists and it is perhaps-
The only Tories there are the hard-shell Grits.

One sometimes wonders about the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) who brought certain legislation in here a couple of years ago which most people in the Atlantic provinces did not think much of.
It seems to me, that in addition to the general development of trade, and in addition particularly to the development of trade in the whole Atlantic area-and I use "Atlantic" now in another and much wider context- there is one area which is naturally complementary to the Atlantic provinces, and that is the whole Caribbean region, and particularly the British West Indies federation and British Guiana, those areas with which there has been a traditional trade. It does seem to me that here we could do a lot more than we are doing. I should like to see a free trade area between Canada and the West Indies

federation. I should like to see a study made, at any rate, of the possibilities of bringing this area within the ambit of the Canadian monetary system, as Newfoundland was before confederation, and I should like to see a much more vigorous development of the technical and other assistance which has already been started in that area, really a development into something like a Colombo plan for that area.
But there is another thing. I am one of those who believes that a fundamental mistake was made in the development of Canada in 1878 when the national policy was adopted. I believe that that has had the effect of concentrating, of centralizing industry and wealth in the area of the lakes and the upper St. Lawrence valley to an inordinate degree, but no one in his senses-I include myself in that category-would say that we could wipe out the tariff and undo the results of those 50 or 60 years of development. We, when we were in office, pursued a line of policy which it is calculated had the effect of reducing the effect of the tariff by about 50 per cent in 22 years.
But to wipe it out suddenly would, of course, create dislocations of a kind that no government, and I would hope no political party, in its senses would contemplate. The Gordon commission did estimate, and they had very competent people to do it, that the effect of the tariff upon cost to consumers was about $1 billion a year and that the cost was very inequitably distributed across the country. It does seem to me that if the people of Canada are going to pay that kind of price for the tariff, the price that the experts have estimated, we should have more say than we do now in the location of industries that are protected and in the national interest an effort should be made not to establish rigid controls and decide that this industry must be put here and that there, but to create certain advantages and inducements that will overcome some of the disadvantages that otherwise exist in certain areas.
