speechtext: Before I present the motion, does any hon. member wish to speak to its content, from the point of view of its having been dealt before.

Mr. Speaker, because of the presence in Ottawa today of some of the leading Canadian labour leaders I had expected the Liberals would decide to raise the issue of unemployment, particularly as it affects the province of British Columbia. However, the members of the C.C.F. group are very happy that the official opposition has raised this issue of the need for action on behalf of the four Atlantic provinces. We readily admit that we have here a real national problem. The economy of the Atlantic region has been ailing for a number of years now, and I believe that no one in Canada would be prepared to lay all the blame for the ills of the Atlantic economic community on the Conservative government today. The ills that exist may, in certain aspects, have worsened within recent years. However, in the main, the ills that are now obvious were especially obvious to the people of the Atlantic area long before this Conservative government assumed office. I believe that was one of the major reasons why most of the people in the Atlantic area decided to vote against the Liberal government back in 1957, and with even more emphasis in 1958.
I am very pleased to see that the Liberals, at least at this late stage, recognize that we have on our hands a problem that is not only of local significance or responsibility, but that we have a difficulty that has to be faced up to by the national government in Ottawa.

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces
The people down there expected a great deal when they upset the Liberal governments within their provinces and the Liberal government at Ottawa. I am afraid that the people there are rapidly coming to the conclusion that they may be waiting in vain for a solution to their difficulties because after this government has been in office now for practically three years there have been extremely limited indications that the government of the day is looking at the problem of the Atlantic region with any more serious concern than that which was evidenced by the Liberal government.
The people of Canada owe much to the people of the Atlantic region. They are people who, along with those of Upper and Lower Canada, founded our nation. Their sons and daughters emigrated and were largely responsible for the development of the larger areas of Canada. Especially did they make a tremendous contribution in that they educated so many of their sons and daughters before they saw them emigrate into other areas of Canada. Many of the western and central Canadian leaders of today were educated at the expense and sacrifice of their parents in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island. These people supplied much of the money that was necessary for the opening up of our nation. They were taxed for our development. A great deal of the investment capital that was originally created in this region was invested in other areas of Canada rather than in the maintenance of its own economic health and welfare. In that regard I feel that any investment on the part of the national government in the Atlantic region is merely paying off the obligation we owe.
I cannot ignore the tremendous contribution they have made to the rest of Canada in the development of the co-operative movement and the credit union movement. However, Mr. Speaker, as has already been indicated, the people in the Atlantic region of Canada are not being allowed to enjoy their full share of the blessings that accrue to Canadians as a whole. They are denied equality of opportunity to share in the development of Canada. Many of them are even unemployed. Certainly, as the statistics have indicated over so many long years, they are not allowed to receive an equitable amount of the riches that are produced in the nation as a whole.
The whole nation is their heritage, as it is of all other Canadians. However, they are being denied their proper portion of that heritage. We note this fact when we look at the levels of wages that exist in this part

of Canada, in four out of our ten Canadian provinces. Their cost of living is almost equal to the cost of living anywhere else. For instance, I am told that in Halifax rents are higher than they are in many other major urban areas of Canada. Nevertheless, wage levels throughout New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland are, by a considerable degree, lower than they are in the other parts of Canada. The fishermen there have never had a standard of living that was anywhere nearly equal to that which obtains for the fishermen of British Columbia. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick agriculture does not receive the same per capita income that it receives in other areas of Canada; and even in the other areas it is low enough indeed, far lower than it ought to be. This Atlantic area has more than its proper share of the unemployed in Canada. There are particular areas in which as many as one half of the able-bodied men are unemployed. Many of them have been unemployed not for half a year but for a year and in some cases for a goodly number of years.
The Atlantic area is not obtaining its portion of the industrial development that is taking place in Canada. As a matter of fact many of their industries are losing out and are having to close their doors, thereby adding to the already aggravated unemployment problem. In this regard I note the great regret that was expressed-and aptly so-by the newspapers in the Atlantic region when the estimates for the present fiscal year were laid before the house in that they noted a large reduction in federal capital expenditures. I believe the Halifax area alone this year can expect some $8 million of a reduction in federal capital expenditures as compared with the amount a year ago. All the statistics are borne out when we look at the per capita income. I note with regret that the people in Nova Scotia, for instance, receive only one half of the per capita income received by the people of Ontario or British Columbia. To me this situation is a violation of one of the concepts of nationhood, when for their work the people of one region of one and the same nation receive a per capita income that is only one half of what is being received elsewhere.
In the field of education I notice that the income of the school teachers is roughly half of what it is in many of the western portions of Canada. In the matter of health services, the governments in the Atlantic region are simply unable to supply the residents with the level of health services existing elsewhere. The Canadian boy or girl has the

same rights to health services and to education, whether that boy or girl is living in Halifax, Toronto or Vancouver. The object of the government ought to be to undertake measures that will ensure equal rights of citizenship to every Canadian, no matter where in Canada he may live.
In looking at this amendment offered by the Liberals I am pleased to note that the Liberals realize that in order to help the Atlantic area to any significant extent the government must embark on a planned program of federal assistance. I think the Liberals are now beginning to move a little way in the direction in which I am sure political needs will make them move much more yet before the next federal election rolls around. In a major undertaking of this kind they are now willing to adopt the idea and the concept that effective help can only be given if it is being given on the basis of a planned program.
We hear a great deal about the prosperity of the nation this year. However, the conditions as they exist in the Atlantic region once again indicate that the so-called prosperity which we have is far too narrowly based in that more regional problems are arising on the Canadian national scene. The Atlantic area is possibly the largest and most needy region with regard to aid in Canada today. As between different parts of Canada, once again the rich are getting richer at a much more rapid rate than the poor are getting less poor.
The recommendations that we see in the amendment calls for the establishment of an Atlantic capital projects program for the purpose of assuring the financing of projects essential to the economic development of the Atlantic provinces. In our opinion this is only the Liberal name for the old C.C.F. name for a national investment board. However, we believe that they now realize the need for the establishment of what would in effect be a national investment board because this Atlantic capital projects program is intended, they say, for the purpose of assuring financing. To rely on the whims of private investors to resolve the capital needs of the Atlantic area would not be very realistic and I am very happy to note that the Liberals realize that action on the part of the federal government toward the raising of the necessary money is necessary.
It is my opinion that for this proposal to be effective a lot of money will have to be spent. I would advocate that the federal government begin initially with an investment in the neighbourhood of $500 million. That may sound like a lot of money, but when we consider that four of the ten Canadian provinces are involved and when we
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces look at the needs of this area of Canada I think the amount I have mentioned of half a billion dollars would be a modest yet effective beginning. Agriculture alone in the Atlantic area can absorb hundreds of millions of investment capital in order to consolidate existing uneconomic units into efficiently operating economic units. Industrial development would be able to absorb at least as much as agriculture.
I would like to underline that an outlay of $500 million for aid in economic development in the Atlantic area would not be a net expense. There would be returned to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlanj a hefty proportion because of added revenue emanating from income tax and the general 11 per cent sales tax. I believe that if an undertaking of this magnitude were launched the people who now live in the Atlantic region would supply a considerable amount of this money because of their own belief that this area needs this assistance.
We are a little worried about the next recommendation which we see in the amendment, the provision of special fiscal incentives to private enterprise for the purpose of encouraging industrial growth. We have noted the encouragement of private enterprise in the investment field, especially as it applies to natural resources in many areas of Canada, and our experiences in this regard have not always been happy. We want to be very careful that when we undertake measures of this kind-and we as a group are not opposed to this recommendation-when this recommendation is implemented, if it is, there ought to go along with it ample protection of the resources for the people to ensure they will not be plundered away from the people. The workers and the farmers and everyone within the area should reap some of the blessings of the exploitation of what is their own heritage. We do not want any Wenner-Grens in the Atlantic area, for instance, and we note with utter dismay how the people of Newfoundland are being exploited and their natural resources used to make multi-millionaires in other areas of the world.
I hope that if the government undertakes incentives to encourage more private enterprise to invest its capital it will also encourage the democratic movements within the area-I have particular reference to labour unions, to farm organizations and to organizations of fishermen-so that the men and women who do the work will receive an adequate return from their resources. Unless there is this kind of economic democracy at the grass roots level whereby people are

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces able to obtain a larger share of their heritage then I am afraid exploitation and regret many years later will be the order of the day.
I noted the omission of many specific recommendations which might have been made in an amendment of this kind. However, I realize that the obvious intent of the amendment is not to clutter it up with too many specific recommendations. I notice nothing which calls upon the government to ensure the survival of the independent small businessman in the Atlantic region. I notice nothing in here for the inclusion of coal as one of the responsibilities of the national energy board. I see nothing for the need of the people of that region for an aggressive policy of vocational training with pay so that the many unemployed would more likely be provided with employment. I notice no reference to the need for education.
On the question of unemployment mention has been made of the coal industry, and I would like at this time to propose that the steel industry which exists in the Atlantic region be not permitted to move out of that region. I think it is simply scandalous that such a great proportion of our iron ore, when we have our own energy in abundance, especially in Nova Scotia, has to be taken right past the door of the Atlantic provinces, down the St. Lawrence seaway. Our energy is exported out of western Canada and iron ore is exported out of eastern Canada to the heart of the United States of America, supplying employment to the United States instead of supplying employment to Canadians. I believe that action on the part of the government may be necessary to ensure the survival of whatever steel industry exists, not only in the interests of those who work in that enterprise but also in the interests of continuing markets for Nova Scotia coal; and because we in Canada are, on balance, even yet importers of steel, I believe there should be established in the Atlantic region additional steel facilities.
It is for these reasons that at this time I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), that the amendment be amended by adding thereto:
5.	The maintenance of the present steel industry in the Atlantic provinces, together with the expansion of the steel industry by every appropriate means including the provision of a publicly owned steel mill.
6.	The active encouragement and strengthening of such peoples' organizations in the Atlantic provinces as farm, fishermen, and labour unions, and the co-operative and credit union movements.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has submitted an amendment to the amendment which seems to go into the provincial field


whereas the initial amendment relates entirely to federal assistance. I raise the question of whether he is not doing more than submitting an amendment but rather submitting what in effect is another motion because, as I understand our practice, the subamendment should come within the scope of the initial amendment.
I assume you have reference to the latter clause?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

May I point out that while in the main these are responsibilities of provincial governments there is also federal responsibility and indeed there exists federal legislation with respect to most of these items. There has been federal participation in respect to all these items. Labour is not exclusively a provincial matter nor are agricultural organizations.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I read the clause about which I have doubt. It is item No. 6, in these words:
6. The active encouragement and strengthening of such peoples' organizations in the Atlantic provinces as farm, fishermen, and labour unions, and the co-operative and credit union movements.
Generally speaking, those organizations in the Atlantic provinces are the subject of provincial jurisdiction although there is to some extent co-ordinate jurisdiction of the federal government.
In that case, if you so rule, I will omit the last clause.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would certainly feel that it would remove the very strong doubt which I have that No. 6 does not come within the scope of the initial amendment. If the hon. member wishes to submit his amendment limiting it to item No. 5, I will accept it.
I so move.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), that the amendment be amended by adding thereto:
5. The maintenance of the present steel industry in the Atlantic provinces, together with the expansion of the steel industry by every appropriate means including the provision of a publicly owned steel mill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas M. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in making a few brief remarks on the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), may I first of all commend him for bringing this matter concerning the Atlantic provinces to the attention of this house. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate enjoys a very good

sense of timing and has displayed it on many occasions. I do not know whether he realizes that today, May 2, has some significance for the maritimes in that it is the birthday of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) and also of my young son, and in a few minutes we would have been toasting this fact. I mention this because the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton is a great maritimer. My son, unfortunately, was not born in the maritimes and will go through life with that handicap.
Just like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. As the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) has said, this is the same disability under which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate operates. I do feel, however, that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has some right to speak on matters relating to the Atlantic provinces because recently a meeting of Conservative members elected him as the man they would most prefer to have speak in their ridings at election time, having realized that in the past election, in every constituency in which the hon. gentleman spoke the Conservative government member was returned. Everyone is aware that provincial elections are coming up and while the federal members may be limited in their participation I do hope that if the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate does decide to travel east and participate in the provincial elections he will make my constituency of Saint John-Albert the very first on his list.
Before the supply motion was brought forward today there was a great deal of speculation as to what would be the subject of the motion. This always occurs on these occasions but I believe that today over 95 per cent of the hon. members of this house would have thought that the Bomarc or national defence would have been the subject of the amendment.
Would the hon. member permit a question. Does he think that would be a suitable subject for a want of confidence motion?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member has many subjects which he feels would be suitable subjects for want of confidence motions but I do not think anyone in this house or in the country worries about them to the same degree he does.
As I mentioned, I believe there were very few hon. members in this house who did not expect that the Bomarc or national defence would be the subject of today's supply motion. But there was one fellow in this chamber, my friend the hon. member for Prince (Mr. 2, 1960
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces Phillips) sitting behind me, who thought differently. I asked him what he thought might be the subject and he said he felt that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-to use the more impersonal, than affectionate term-was probably going to bring forward an amendment concerning the Atlantic provinces. I admit that this thought had not crossed my mind but as I glanced across the aisle and saw the determined, supercilious and perhaps even courageous expression on the face of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I knew we were in for something today.
Perhaps I use the word "courageous" advisedly because I think it took a great deal of courage on the part of the hon. member to stand up in this house, knowing a bit of the background of this subject of the maritime provinces, and speak on it. He knows, as we all do, the history that goes back over a period of 22 years of absolute neglect of the maritime provinces. When he makes a statement that the time has now arrived for action, that is when I say he certainly deserves full marks for courage because he knows that the time arrived in 1957. He knows, as does everyone in this house and in the country, that we constantly pressed the previous administration in an effort to have it pay some attention to the problems of those provinces by the sea, but we met with no success.
One could mention many matters, but the subject that I feel the opposition party, the former government, is most vulnerable on is the matter of Beechwood. After the second world war we realized in the maritimes that our main difficulties were power and transportation. We had not shared in the federal war contracts and we had gone even further behind at that time. We said that we would come to Ottawa and make approaches regarding our power situation. The former Liberal government of New Brunswick came here without any definite proposals but they did talk about power. What did they get? They got no attention whatsoever from their fellow members here at Ottawa.
History began, Mr. Speaker, in 1952 when we changed to a new Conservative government under Premier Hugh John Flemming of New Brunswick. He, realizing the great need for power in our province and in the maritimes, at once began his campaign to bring this matter to the attention of the powers that be at Ottawa, the then old, tired Liberal administration. It was not a case of merely receiving a no answer, Mr. Speaker; it was not a case of indifference; it was a complete cold shoulder on every single occasion that this matter was mentioned on the many trips of Premier Flemming to Ottawa.

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces
I could also mention the indifference of the former minister of finance, Mr. Harris, who on every occasion not only said "no", but would not even discuss the various thoughts that we had about power and other financial matters. Yes, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate certainly deserves a lot of credit for courage in bringing this matter forward today, knowing the background of his party on this subject of Atlantic provinces' assistance.
We also note that when this government took over in 1957 one of its first acts was to deal with this matter of Beechwood. Today we have in New Brunswick on the Saint John river an everlasting monument to the promises made by this government.
Will the hon. member permit a question? In what year was Beechwood built?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Beechwood was completed last year and we were all down at the ceremony; hon. members from the opposition were present as well.
Will the hon. member tell the house at what stage Beechwood was when this government came into office?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not certain of the date, but the point is that the old government would have nothing to do with the financial arrangements for Beechwood. I sat in this house, when the former member for Charlotte, a member of the Liberal party, got up at that time and said he was definitely opposed to Beechwood in every aspect. This government definitely financed, in every way that they had promised, the Beechwood project in New Brunswick and that is the significant part. We did something about the power problems at Beechwood and in our later power assistance for the mari-times and the Atlantic provinces.
I come now to the second matter that I mentioned. One does not have to be an historian, like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, to know that one of our other difficulties was transportation. We acted, on transportation. After many cries while in the Conservative opposition we set up a royal commission to deal with the freight rate problem, and that commission is now sitting and has been sitting for many weeks. It is considering our problems and I hope something will come forward that will assist us in the future.

Will the hon. member permit a question at this point? Will the hon. member recall that while this government set

up a royal commission we increased the subvention under the Maritime Freight Rates Act from 20 per cent to 30 per cent, that is by 50 per cent?
And also increased the freight rates by 20 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member mentioned that in his speech and it is quite true. But he did mention in connection with the freight rate increase that the 7 per cent applied only to the Atlantic provinces. The 7 per cent is a horizontal increase across the country. I do recognize that part of it, anyway, Mr. Speaker.
The Chignecto canal project has been talked about for many years but the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate shied clear of that even though he did mention it once or twice in questions on the orders of the day. But the present government on coming into office, and in connection with promises that were made, set up surveys, both engineering and economic, to deal with the Chignecto canal. This is something again that I say makes me wonder about this courage that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate shows in bringing this forward today when he knows that for at least 22 years they failed to act in this regard.
I now want to deal with my constituency of Saint John-Albert. I do not wish to indicate great knowledge on the various subjects of fish, agriculture and power. This reminds me that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate sat in this house and opposed the federal power proposition last year. Now he has enough nerve to get up and quote speeches advocating unity amongst the maritime members.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I know the hon. member is allowing his enthusiasm to run away with him but if he will examine the votes he will find that I supported and voted for the Atlantic power legislation of this government, which carried out the policy announced by Mr. Harris in 1957. My only complaint was that it did not apply to Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not need to apologize for my enthusiasm in so far as the maritimes are concerned. I think quite modestly that it is a better type of enthusiasm than the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate displays. Incidentally, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson), in speaking about this matter, said to me he was glad to see that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was now back in
34G7

the maritimes and might leave the matter of the station at Flin Flon, Manitoba alone for a while to some people who know something about it.
I do wish to refer particularly to my constituency of Saint John-Albert, and it is an occasion I have been waiting for for some time, to mention the great prosperity that we have in Saint John. While I may not be qualified to speak with great knowledge on financial matters, I do feel that I can speak as one from an area in the maritimes that since 1957 has prospered and has gone forward under this government to the nth degree. We had our problems of power and of transportation, as I have mentioned. I feel that the prosperity that the city of Saint John is now enjoying-and one that will be welcome by everyone in Canada-is due definitely to the actions that have been taken by the new government. It may be that certain matters of direct assistance have not been given but after all we are living in a private enterprise economy and it is the duty of the government to provide the means for private enterprise to go forward, and I say that this government has given this means, particularly to Saint John.
I wish to quote from an editorial in the Saint John Tele graph-Journal of February 9. It is a reliable editorial. This is a newspaper, that has lately been criticizing this government in many respects but in straightforwardly telling this case I feel that we will have the answer as to the status of a certain area in the Atlantic provinces. I quote:
Saint John, 175 years old and long the Industrial centre of the maritime provinces-
I do not know whether my friends from Halifax will agree with that but proportionately we have always had a great deal of industry
-entered a new era of booming expansion in the late 1950's, an era which is destined to see the city reach an unprecedented level of prosperity in the decade ahead. Never in her long history have prospects been so good for this seaport city, transportation centre and hub of industry. Never before has this proud loyalist city had reason to flex her muscles with such commanding authority. Never, in fact, has the mushrooming area of greater Saint John experienced such a period of boisterous expansion and optimism. Major capital expenditures of the last three years far exceed $100 million and many, many more millions are to be spent on expansion in the years immediately ahead.
The whole metropolitan area is riding the crest of a wave of construction never matched since the United Empire Loyalists set foot on the peninsula in 1783 and founded the city two years later. All over greater Saint John-Saint John, Lancaster and Simonds-a wealth of new building is evidence of the new prosperity. Industry and government are spending many millions in long term projects. Businesses are expanding and adding
2, 1960
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces new plants and equipment. Communications are multiplying, with new roads either just completed or under way at every city approach-
The special article goes on to tell the story of Saint John and explains in better words than I could use Why I feel that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate does not know what he is talking about and should make the visit to Saint John which I mentioned a moment ago. To be more specific, I should like to outline some of the private enterprise capital projects that have been completed and are listed here. I will start by mentioning those that are of a private enterprise nature.
First, we have the $50 million Irving Oil refinery in Simonds. May I say that in reading an article this morning in connection with the Encyclopedia Britannica I noted that the city of Calgary has a new oil refinery that will deliver 14,700 barrels a day and that it is the greatest capital project they have ever had in their city. The refinery we have in Saint John will deliver 43,000 barrels a day.
The second project is a kraft mill, lumber mill and pulp mill extension by Irving Pulp and Paper Limited, with a total investment of $40 million. The third is the new $7 million paper mill of Kimberly-Clark Limited. The fourth is a new steel works and foundry built for Ocean Steel and Construction Limited. Then there are several new plants on Lancaster's Fairville boulevard, now known as the golden mile. There is a long list of about 10 other items involving capital projects of a nature that I feel will be envied by every member of the house.
There has also been a tremendous development so far as government projects are concerned. New government buildings and wharves, for which we waited 22 years under the old Liberal government, have been constructed. In 1957 when we took office these projects were commenced and now they are ready for business.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate did make some very good points in his so-called non-political speech. He made certain remarks about the West Indies to which I feel attention should be called. Having just returned from a commonwealth parliamentary association meeting there over the Easter recess, I recognize the need for greater attention to that area. Efforts should be made to strengthen our traditional ties and to foster greater trade expansion. In so far as our connections with the West Indies are concerned, we miss the C.N.S. ships. It is true that our trade with the West Indies has been going ahead but it has been more of a natural growth. I would certainly want to be associated with the remarks of the hon. member
3468	HOUSE OF
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces for Bonavista-Twillingate about paying more attention to the West Indies federation.
It may be that we should put forward some proposals regarding free trade. Having been there and talked to many representatives of the West Indies federation, I do not have the answer, but I do know that it is in Canada's interests not only from the point of view of trade benefit but as a commonwealth country to give all aspects of the situation in the West Indies even closer attention.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do want to say that there is a lesson that the new West Indies federation has to learn. We made reference to it in our speeches there and in our discussions about the difficulties of the federation. We pointed out the fact that Canada had poor and rich areas and that a great deal of consideration had to be given to those areas which do not come up to the national average economically speaking. In Canada we have some areas that are not as wealthy as others. In its very early stages the West Indies federation is beginning to realize that there will be great difficulties in that some of the islands will probably never be as wealthy as the large ones such as Jamaica and Trinidad.
I mention this merely to point out that this is a problem we have recognized in Canada and it is one that they must recognize. It is a problem that we must always be watching here. In the speeches that were made at the conference reference was made to the fact that our central provinces continually have to be making what they call concessions to the poorer areas in order to bring up the average. I am one who feels that by some method greater concessions will have to be made.
But I do want to say that so far as the new government is concerned, by Beechwood, by federal power assistance, by transportation investigation and by fiscal measures such as the special adjustment grants we have gone forward and done many of the things we promised, things that were not only forgotten for 22 years but were given the cold shoulder completely.
With regard to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I want to say that there is a gross inconsistency in it. In his speech he referred to the fact that he was against the principle of the special adjustment grants. I am surprised to hear anybody representing the Atlantic provinces stand up in the house and say that he is against the special adjustment


grants, particularly a member from Newfoundland which, pro rata, gains a little bit more than the other Atlantic provinces from the adjustment grants.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, once more the hon. gentleman's enthusiasm has outrun his accuracy. I said no such thing. I said and I have always said that I was in favour of them and I only wished that the principle could be extended so that it would apply to any province in need.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Unless I
heard the hon. member incorrectly, Mr. Speaker, he stated that the former member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare said that this was a form of deficiency payment and he went on to derogate the adjustment grants.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Whether he said he was opposed to them, I do not know. As far as I am concerned, if this principle does not meet with the approval of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate then his amendment does not agree with his thinking because the whole amendment is full of special considerations. As a member from the Atlantic provinces, from the constituency of Saint John-Albert which is doing well, I want to say that while I go along with special adjustment grants and some other special considerations I certainly would not want to be associated with them to the degree that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has put them forward today.

They are exactly as in
the advertisement containing the Atlantic resolutions, in which advertisement your picture also appeared.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
You may say
so, but I do not take a back seat in supporting the Atlantic resolutions. We have fulfilled many of them and many more will be fulfilled before the hon. member knows how to say Jack Robinson.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or Jack Pickersgill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Jack Pickersgill, as the Minister of Finance has said.
I also want to say that in this amendment put forward by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mention is made of transportation difficulties. We are dealing with the transportation difficulties now, after having waited 22 years for the Liberals to do something about them. We have undertaken surveys of the Chignecto canal and other matters. There is a royal commission sitting now on

all our transportation difficulties. The commission deals particularly with rail transportation, but its terms of reference also have other implications.
The C.C.F. party has moved a subamendment, and as usual it is so involved in-I do not know what you would call it-state enterprise, that it is impossible to figure it out. Someone said that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) likes to chide Conservative members by saying that the only part of Canada in which the C.C.F. party has no representation is the most backward part, that is the maritimes. All I can say is that we do not want the C.C.F. party, anyway. If they show themselves in these two provincial elections, which have prompted the speech by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I am sure they will again get a goose egg.

The amendment which I had the privilege of seconding deals with a matter of far-reaching importance, not only to the Atlantic provinces but also to all parts of Canada because, as has been said so often, no nation can flourish to the extent it could and should flourish when any segment of it is a depressed area. This is the situation with respect to the Atlantic provinces in the Canadian nation. This situation is more disturbing because at the time of confederation this was a flourishing community which joined this nation to make a bigger and better nation. This action brought about the direct opposite over the years.
The retarded economy of the Atlantic provinces is a subject which is receiving many comments in periodicals all across Canada, a subject which has been brought to the attention of the government and the public through many channels, by editorial comment, by speakers in chambers of commerce, boards of trade, service clubs, and by other means. Lately there has been a strong awakening amongst the people of the Atlantic provinces as to their present position in the Canadian community, and keener concern as to their future. This stronger awakening and keener concern has brought about more serious thinking and action on the part of groups and individuals, with the Atlantic provinces' press urging government action, with timely and well considered planned programs of action aimed at bringing about these things that are necessary to ensure that the Atlantic provinces' place in our confederation is close to the Canadian average.
The adverse position of the Atlantic provinces is being recognized more and more by Canadians in the other six provinces. The Canadian press of central and western Canada have also taken up the plea for an improved 79951-0-219
2, 1960
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces economy for the provinces on the Atlantic coast. With the widespread movement for concerted action to bring about an improvement in the Atlantic region it is timely that this amendment to the supply motion be placed before the House of Commons because it provides an opportunity for a two-day debate on a matter which is one of the most important facing Canada on the home front.
Many appeals have been made, and from many sources, for unity amongst all Atlantic province members of parliament in the matter of aid to the Atlantic region. A prominent Canadian journalist expressed the view that the problems of the Atlantic provinces should be aired vigorously, and the only effective place in which that could be done was on the floor of the House of Commons, where every voice raised strengthened the case and pricked the conscience of those who forgot the Atlantic provinces. The case is for unanimity on the part of all Atlantic provinces members. Neglect of this region cannot continue if all members from the Atlantic provinces with one voice call for a program of required assistance. I should like to add that this view was expressed by a journalist from central Canada.
This unanimity should be expressed by all Atlantic members, without reservation, in the initial stages of the planning. When the necessary data has been compiled it is conceivable that there will be internal disagreements which will have to be worked out, if a program is to be developed that will bring about the over-all desired result without having a serious adverse effect on any area. Action cannot be postponed much longer without a still more serious situation developing. Whatever is done must be done without further delay. The action taken will, of necessity, have to be something exceptional, something never undertaken before.
The Gordon commission, in its supplementary report on the retarded economy of the Atlantic provinces, stated as a general conclusion:
The long term and ultimately effective solution of the problem must be expected to come from further resource development. The core of the problem is the creation of conditions which will attract capital into such development.
It was unfortunate that the solemn pledges made by Conservative federal candidates in the 1957 election campaign and repeated in the 1958 campaign, called the Atlantic resolutions, died a hurried death. I feel that I should express the view that probably some of those candidates who were in the political arena for the first time felt that those promises and pledges would be as vigorously promoted in parliament as they were on

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces the hustings, in government as well as in opposition. The candidates who were not successful at the polls have not the same onus, or the same opportunity, to promote these pledges. It is the duty of those elected, who so pledged themselves-and there are 21 of them-to vigorously promote the solemn promises made.
No doubt many of the Conservative members from the Atlantic provinces elected for the first time in 1957 and 1958 felt that all the things that were promised would materialize. They probably waited for their senior colleagues to lead the fight, particularly their four senior colleagues who became cabinet members representing the four Atlantic provinces. These same members who cried out when in opposition for the very things they later promised to do in the Atlantic resolutions have failed to promote any action toward bringing about those things that are recognized as essential for the improvement and future stability of the Atlantic provinces.
Let us take a look at the pledges made in the Atlantic resolutions, a charter drafted by the 31 Conservative candidates in the Atlantic provinces during a meeting and released to the press in the form of large advertisements on June 4, 1957, just six days before election day that year. These advertisements were headed, "Before You Vote Read 'The Atlantic Resolutions' A subheading in the advertisement states that the promises were endorsed by every Progressive Conservative candidate in the maritimes. I wonder why this subheading did not include the Newfoundland members? The opening paragraph, following the subheading entitled "Atlantic Resolutions", included the names of all 31 Conservative candidates in the Atlantic provinces.
The most significant heading in the advertisement, most significant in view of the fact the action promised has not been taken in the three-year period, is the heading entitled "A Call for United Action at Ottawa".
In view of what has taken place since June 10, 1957, one is led to believe that the Atlantic resolutions were drafted with the view held by the Atlantic Conservative candidates that the Tory party would still be in opposition.
The seven resolutions were entitled: National resources development program, Decentralization of industry, Atlantic provinces power development, Transportation, Capital projects program, Fiscal needs of the Atlantic provinces and Canadian coastguard.
I hasten to give credit to the government for the financial assistance rendered in

special grants to the Atlantic provinces. It would be unfair not to give credit for this action as it materially assisted these provinces.
What has taken place in respect of some of the other Atlantic resolutions has been put into proper perspective by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). Other hon. members speaking for this party will deal with the Atlantic resolutions and with other matters of vital importance to the other Atlantic provinces.
Let me bring to the attention of the house a few of the statements contained in the Atlantic resolutions advertisements beyond the headings and subheadings I have listed. I believe that the vast majority of the hon. members of this house are not familiar with the document which is under discussion and I suggest they read the resolutions and decide where the onus lies. I quote from the leading paragraph:
We-
Which means the 31 Conservative candidates.
-are resolved to stand together in support of these measures-
The measures being the ones which I have just enumerated under the seven headings.
____which will help to overcome the historic disabilities which have limited and even denied opportunity to this area.
The same leading paragraph states:
We the Progressive Conservative candidates from the 31 federal constituencies in the Atlantic provinces, believe the Just demands of the Atlantic community for recognition of their economic problems and special needs urgently require more united and forceful representation in the parliament of Canada.
Let me repeat the latter part of this quotation:
-urgently require more united and forceful representation in the province of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what is being done today by the official opposition and in view of the statements in the Atlantic resolutions it is hard to conceive that the amendment will not receive the support of all Atlantic provinces members. I feel sure that the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne) will support the amendment as he has been the only Atlantic Conservative member to demand action for the Atlantic provinces from the government on these resolutions.
The Atlantic resolutions is a good document. What is unfortunate is that it was never put into effect, that it apparently was used for a particular purpose at a particular time and then was forgotten about. It certainly had a great appeal to the voters in the maritime provinces and was an instrument by

which a very large measure of party support was secured at the polls. When solemn promises are made to the electors in a public document, those who make the promises and are elected have a solemn duty vigorously to demand in parliament and outside parliament that the promises be implemented. These demands have been found wanting.
The onus for bringing about the Atlantic resolutions rests primarily with the four Atlantic provinces cabinet ministers. They are members of the group that decide upon government policies. They are the four representatives to whom the people of the Atlantic region look for, and from whom they expect-yes, demand-leadership in the promotion and enactment of the Atlantic resolutions, in the drafting of which they played a major role. If the four Atlantic cabinet ministers lead in these demands on the floor of this chamber I am sure they will receive the complete support of all Atlantic provinces members of both parties and, I venture to say, the support of the majority of the hon. members of this house.
What contributes to the present economy in the Atlantic provinces? Federal government projects that contribute to the economy of the province of New Brunswick were all established by the former Liberal government and the same statement applies to the other Atlantic provinces. The large military camp at Gagetown is an important factor in the economy of the Fredericton-Saint John area. The Department of National Defence is by far the largest single employer of civilians in Northumberland-Miramichi and together with air force personnel is the backbone of the economy of this area. The R.C.A.F. jet operational and training base at Chatham, the R.C.A.F. radar station at St. Margarets and the naval ammunition depot at Renous were all established by the former government as was the army ordnance depot at McGivney in the adjoining county of York.
This government has not placed a single labour-employing establishment in the province of New Brunswick. A comparison of Department of Public Works and other departmental estimates for the past three years, with those of previous years under the former government shows drastic cut-backs in expenditures for New Brunswick.
Where did the hon. member get those figures?

They are in the book of
estimates.
No.

The hon. member can check the matter and he will find that what I have said is correct.
