Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces
A realistic approach has not been taken by this government toward long awaited adequate economic and engineering surveys of the Atlantic seaway and the Northumberland strait causeway. I say that a realistic approach has not been taken and it is evident, from the answers to questions as found in Hansard, that the surveys are more or less of a superficial nature, despite the promises made in 1957 and 1958 that full scale surveys would be carried out immediately.
Members of the Liberal party have listed for government action, as can be found in Hansard, many proposals considered to be for the benefit of the Atlantic region. One of these proposals is improvement in the highway transportation system. The Liberal party at its last convention endorsed a policy of an adequate highway system for the Atlantic provinces.
An adequate highway system is a dire need for the north and east area of New Brunswick. In this area where lumbering, fishing and farming are the chief industries and where there is a potential base metal mining industry there is a vital need of good roads for the development of these industries and the facilities with which to transport the products to distributing centres and on to their markets. Toward this end the government should promote a second trans-Canada highway, together with a network of connecting highways, needed to give incentive for investment of capital with a resultant expansion.
In the 1860's railways were required to open up the maritime provinces. In the 1960's the requirement for industrial and tourist expansion is highways. Today the maritime rail passenger services are being curtailed. Many of these services have been or are about to be eliminated or reduced. Highway transport has taken over the bulk of transportation, with the exception of carload lot shipments. Railway employees are continually being laid off, a fact which is indicative of the trend to highway transportation. Mail and express shipments are being transported over highways. All of these things point to the need for a better system of highways and connecting roads.
The foreseeable economic future of the Atlantic provinces gets more disturbing as time goes on. More and more of our young people are leaving the area in search of employment. While many are returning because they cannot find employment elsewhere, still many more never return a loss that cannot be reconciled. This exodus is due to the alarming unemployment situation in most parts of the Atlantic region. This situation is most acute in this area. It creates

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces a problem that affects the very root of family existence. It is a problem that is crying out for remedy and a problem that must have adequate action and co-operation at all levels of government.
Despite the exodus from the Atlantic provinces the unemployment situation has reached alarming proportions. The "Do it now, don't wait for spring" campaign met with no success in most areas of the Atlantic region. The present situation in many parts of this area is that hopes are dim for even a fair scale of employment this summer, the results of which will not reach their full impact until next winter. Is the next campaign slogan to be the opposite: "We didn't do it this year, wait until next year"?
The future economy of the Atlantic provinces looks bleaker as time goes on. More people are wondering if joining confederation was as good a move as was anticipated. It has not brought about the improvements that were envisaged, improvements that would compensate for some of the losses. The situation today reminds us of the misgivings voiced by men in public life at the time of the conference preceding confederation. No Canadians are more loyal than maritime Canadians. Our forefathers played a great role in making the Canadian nation and their descendants are proud of the contribution. Will the generation to come hold that same pride? I trust that action will be taken to preserve this pride for all time.
The maritime provinces area at the time of confederation was a flourishing community with good future prospects. It had a high Canadian average of income and standard of living for that day. Today the average Atlantic family income is away below the Canadian average and the per capita income is also away below the Canadian average. In 1955 the Gordon commission report compiled the family income at 31 per cent below the Canadian average and the per capita income at 37 per cent below the Canadian average.
The people of the Atlantic provinces are bearing their share of the Canadian contributions to underprivileged areas of the world and are pleased, I am sure, to have a part in this great humanitarian work. The Atlantic provinces are Canada's own underdeveloped area. The development of the Atlantic provinces is a national task calling for the application of national policies designed and tailored for this specific purpose and not merely the application of policies which are applied uniformly across Canada.
Much is heard these days about the best way to celebrate the one hundredth birthday of confederation seven years away. Surely
tMr. McWilliam.i
the best way would be to take measures to make sure that by 1967 the people of the Atlantic provinces will have equal reason with residents of the other six provinces to rejoice, to be proud and to be fully satisfied to be a Canadian.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have the opportunity of taking part in this debate on this most interesting subject. I certainly appreciate the broad line of non-partisan motives which inspired the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) to bring forward this resolution at this time. I would say it is only a mere coincidence that an election was announced in Nova Scotia last week and that it is rumoured in various newspapers and elsewhere that there may be other elections forthcoming in the maritimes in the immediate future. That, as I said, is one of those mere coincidences which only happens in the politics of the maritime provinces.
I also appreciate the broadminded and nonpartisan speech, which went a little further to emphasize its non-partisanship, which has been delivered by the hon. member for North-umberland-Miramichi (Mr. McWilliam). It certainly was one of the most non-partisan speeches, and so non-partisan that I think it was a preliminary warm-up to a statement to be read on every platform in his constituency during the provincial election when he goes down to take part in it.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred to the Atlantic resolutions, and he inferred, of course, that hon. members on this side of the house would naturally give support to a motion which included in it part of the language of those Atlantic resolutions. Naturally we on this side of the house and our friends on the other side will always give support to the Atlantic resolutions. As has been said, we drafted and prepared them; we have largely implemented them and we are going to stay in office until we conclude the implementation of them. The hon. member is perhaps laying a little land mine there in order to say that these terrible Tories said something one day, and then some time later he will point out where we voted against it in the resolution now before the house.
Everyone can read and everyone knows that this is a vote of non-confidence. What-every language may be included in this resolution immediately before us, the resolution is one which we cannot accept, because if we did accept it as a vote of non-confidence it would result in the defeat of this government. Of course, it would only be defeated in the house because when we went to the

country we would be re-elected. But the result of any action which would restore hon. members opposite to the seat of power is such that we could not even continue our support of such a motion. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who had read these Atlantic resolutions of two years ago with shocked surprise and who should know how little had been done, reminded me very much of the tale of Rip Van Winkle who slept in peace for 22 years and then came out of his sleep and suddenly realized what should have been done and what had not been done during the time he was asleep.
May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, when the
house rose at six o'clock I was making some casual reference to my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate having had an experience comparable to that of Rip Van Winkle who wakened after his long sleep and expressed surprise at what had happened in the meantime. Perhaps it would be equally accurate to use Saul of Tarsus as a simile because on the road to Damascus he kicked against the pricks and saw a great light. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate after having spent three years in opposition has now undoubtedly seen a great light and speaks and acts far differently from those days when he sat on this side of the house.
Whatever may be the merits of any case the hon. gentleman presents in this house one always admires his skill as a debater in presenting the facts as he would like to have them presented, minimizing those things he does not want to be recognized and magnifying those things that should not be magnified at all. Never is he better at that than when he makes reference in fair terms-he always wishes to be fair-and then pays his respects with a slight tone of praise in his voice to the Atlantic provinces adjustments grants which he says are a good thing and then proceeds immediately thereafter to exaggerate many other matters and attacks the government for all the things it has failed to do. The hon. member reminds one in some ways of the doctor who had been dismissed by a patient who was dying of leukemia. A new doctor was summoned, diagnosed the illness, prescribed treatment and soon had the patient well on the road to recovery. When the patient had his health restored the old doctor who had been dismissed came along, examined the
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces patient who was recovering, and said: "Your doctor did not do much for you; it is true that you are looking well and have regained your health and strength but you are not as big as Goliath; if I had been able to recognize the illness you had and prescribe treatment I would have been able to restore your health and make you well and strong again."
The economy of the Atlantic provinces has not yet attained the status of a Goliath but it is well on the way to recovery. There are many things which need to be done in those provinces. The Conservative members on this side of the house and the four cabinet ministers from that area to whom more than one reference was made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate are fully conscious of the fact that there is much left to be done but we also recognize that a great deal has been accomplished during the last three years, very much more than had been accomplished in any comparable period in the history of those provinces.
I wish to refer to the maritimes adjustment grants to which the hon. member pays such slight praise. After all, they represented only a grant of $25 million a year for four years, or $100 million in all. I realize that $100 million is not a staggering sum of money these days but it is a substantial sum of money for the economy of the Atlantic provinces. This year the province of which I am proud to be a native son had a slight surplus. I have forgotten the exact figure but it amounted to a few hundred thousand. Also, it is budgeting for a surplus of a very few thousand next year. In the meantime, it has increased its payments to municipalities by several millions of dollars, and it has embarked on various other services. Where would those government services be today were it not for the Atlantic provinces grants which have been received by that government from this government?
The same thing can be said, of course, for each one of the other Atlantic provinces. All of them have been able to improve the standard of services, maintain that standard, and balance their budgets. Without those grants they would not have been able to carry on at all, let alone introduce improvements. From the political and fiscal standpoint the grants have represented the difference between life and death. That is what this government has accomplished in that field in a very short time.
I do not propose tonight to clutter up the record with a lot of figures. We all realize that figures can be used in various ways, always fairly of course, but that various interpretations can be placed upon them. I also realize that this is probably only the

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces overture to what will be said time and time again during the next few weeks in at least some of the provinces in the Atlantic area, and I expect that I may be called upon on one or two occasions to make some slight contribution to the ensuing argument. I therefore do not intend tonight to go into detail in this respect nor to build up the record as it will undoubtedly be built up during the next few weeks at least in so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned.
There are facts, however, that are worthy of mention. Not only were these adjustment payments made of $100 million but there were increases in revenue in other ways. There were unconditional payments made to the Atlantic provinces to which I think attention should be drawn. For a moment or two I should like to put some of these figures on the record. I am now going to cover the four Atlantic provinces with respect to the amounts of these unconditional grants.
Unconditional payments to Newfoundland in 1957-58 amounted to $19 million; in 195859, under this government, they had increased to $41 million. Unconditional payments to Prince Edward Island in 1957-58, in the budget which was the last budget brought in by our friends who were then the government, were $4.8 million; in 195859 they had increased to $7.5 million. Unconditional payments to Nova Scotia which in 1957-58 were $29 million had jumped in 1958-59 to $37 million. Unconditional payments to New Brunswick which in 1957-58 Were $23 million had jumped in 1958-59 to $32 million. In the aggregate the total of these unconditional payments to the four Atlantic provinces amounted to $76 million in 1957-58 and had jumped to $117.5 million in 1958-59. The increase amounted to $40.5 million or 58 per cent; I repeat that, 58 per cent.
Would the hon. member permit a question just about the figures? Does not the figure for Newfoundland include two years' instalments of the Newfoundland adjustment grant paid in that particular year?
I think that is probably right and so the figure should be adjusted accordingly.
Yes, downward.

I thank the hon. member for bringing that to my attention. The increase was 58 per cent taking cognizance of the fact which the hon. member drew to my attention. On the other hand, the increase in the unconditional grants to the other six provinces amounted to only $33 million or 10 per cent. That is the rather striking figure to

which I wanted to draw the attention of this house, a 58 per cent increase in unconditional grants to the four Atlantic provinces as compared with a 10 per cent increase in the unconditional grants to the other provinces of Canada.
Of course, we must also consider the conditional grants. In 1957-58 these amounted to $26 million and in 1958-59 they jumped to $49 million. In the year just closed they amounted to something over $68 million. This is an increase of 160 per cent in a two-year period.
These are some of the figures to which attention should be drawn, when my hon. friend asks, or other hon. members ask, what have you done? I ask them to look at that record. When one considers the period through which this country and this government were passing, a recession, and all of the other problems, the record of this government with respect to the Atlantic provinces is something which no one needs to apologize for when an attack is made. I am sure it is something that the Atlantic provinces can look at with a great deal of pride.
Those are the purely fiscal payments; there have been many other payments made as well. Much has been done in other fields. Something was said about industry. I am not going to embark now on a discussion which my hon. friend and I have entered upon from time to time in the past and perhaps will again as to what was proposed by the former government shortly before its demise with respect to assistance to the coal industry and the establishment of industry in the Atlantic provinces, and as to what was done by this government. Suffice it to say that under this government a system of moving Nova Scotia coal, maritime coal but primarily Nova Scotia coal, by subventions, to industrial sites in the maritimes for the development of power was inaugurated, and those subventions were fixed at a level which it is estimated would enable power to be produced at a seven mill rate, and I am advised, without being an expert at all on engineering matters, that a seven mill rate would compare favourably, if not very favourably, with the power rate in Ontario from thermal sources. That should go a long way toward meeting one of the demands which has been heard in the Atlantic provinces for a long time, namely the necessity of getting lower cost power so that industry could be attracted there.
This government, under the legislation and coal subventions, up until this year has paid out over $3,540,000 for the movement of coal for industrial purposes.
Is that within the Atlantic provinces?
Yes, within the Atlantic provinces.
Not outside?

No. Also, in the construction of power lines, transmission lines, a grid system which is envisaged within the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, millions of dollars have been paid out. This money has been paid out in the establishment of those transmission lines so that all of the sources of power on the mainland from Nova Scotia to New Brunswick will be linked together in one grid system, enabling power to flow from one source to the other as it is required.
Last year my colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton), placed some figures on the record. I am not going to weary the house with figures tonight, but anyone who is interested will find them in Hansard of June 10, 1959, at page 4507. It is a long list of figures showing what this government has done in the establishment of various projects such as I have referred to, and particularly the transmission lines. Over $6 million was spent on this last year and a further $13 million has been pledged. Of that $13 million I understand that now the expenditures, although not complete, have run up to about $12 million. That system consists of the establishment of those transmission lines throughout the maritime provinces so that power can be transferred back and forth, thereby helping to establish an industrial life in those provinces which has not been possible before.
One could go on and develop this argument at great length but I know there are many other hon. members who wish to take part in this debate and I do not wish to interfere with them by dealing with matters that some of the others would like to deal with.
This afternoon the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. McWilliam) referred to highways. He made a good provincial speech, outlining the need for more highways in New Brunswick. Undoubtedly, highways are necessary, Mr. Speaker; perhaps more money should be spent on highways; but in addition to the moneys which had been promised under the Trans-Canada Highway Act this government has also established a system of building highways to resources in the various provinces of Canada. Of this amount the maritime provinces, regardless of their size, the fact that they are very small in area and in population, are receiving the same grants as are the larger provinces of
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces Canada. Each province is receiving $7,500,000 from the federal government, and an equal amount from the provincial government, the money to be spent over a period of years. The period was originally fixed at five years but at the request of the provincial governments this period has been extended to a time agreed upon among the various provinces. Although it will not result of course, in all of the highways being reconstructed or built, it is a substantial contribution toward the solution of a problem which the provincial governments have not had the means to deal with adequately. When I hear someone talk, as the hon. member did this afternoon, about the need for highways, I think we should indicate here again the amount of money we shall be getting in the maritime provinces within the next five or six years for the construction of highways and the reconstruction of highways, without which money it would have been impossible for the provinces to have dealt with those problems.
One of the great problems of my province in so far as its industrial life is concerned- not only of its industrial life but its agricultural life as well-is wrapped up to a great extent with the industrial area of the eastern part of the province, the coal fields and the steel mills of Cape Breton island, or the steel mills of Cape Breton island and the coal fields of Cape Breton and of the eastern part of the province.
Much has been said in this house about what has happened to coal during the time this government has been in power. Questions are asked from time to time as to when mines are going to close, and a picture has been painted of the coal industry of Nova Scotia being in a very deplorable state indeed, and the inference is left that the responsibility for this to some extent, at any rate, or to a large extent rests on the shoulders of the governments, provincial and federal. The truth of the matter is, of course, that the coal industry all over the world is in a very bad shape. Coal is being supplanted by other forms of fuel and, particularly in this country, by oil and gas which are natural Canadian products and which are entitled to a share of the market. The fact remains that despite the competition of those fuels it can be safely said that the coal industry of Nova Scotia has come through this period in a better way than have the coal fields of any other part at least of the North American continent.
We also, of course, had the problem aggravated in the last year or two by high water levels and an increase in hydroelectric development and various other factors which have depreciated the market for coal in some

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces ways on a temporary basis and in other ways on other than a temporary basis. These figures are rather interesting. The coal consumed in Canada during the fiscal year just ended amounted to 22,495,000 tons, the smallest tonnage of coal burned in this country since the industrial revolution took place. While the imports of bituminous coal fell from 20,180,000 tons in 1956-57 to only 11,-
800.000	tons last year, the production of Nova Scotia coal increased-I want the house to get this-from 5,701,000 tons to 5,806,000 tons, not a very substantial increase, it is true, but an increase of 105,000 tons when markets for coal were shrinking and falling all around the world and imports of coal into Canada were falling by this substantial amount. Is it any wonder that the market fell? Five years ago the domestic market consumed
6.700.000	tons of bituminous coal; in the year just ended it consumed only 4,600,000 tons. Five years ago the railways consumed 5,-
850,000	tons of coal but in the year just ended they consumed 750,000 tons, a drop of over five million tons. The total consumption of bituminous coal five years ago was 33 million tons and last year only 15 million tons.
There has been a falling off in the demand for coal but in the face of this collapsing market this government, with the assistance and co-operation of the government of Nova Scotia in providing subventions to a certain extent, by the provision of increased amounts of assistance, has managed to provide a remarkable degree of protection for the maritime coal industry. This has largely been established by the assistance of the movement of maritime coal into the province of Ontario. Three years ago, when the severity of the competition from other fuels was first felt, there were 109,000 tons of coal moved into Ontario at a cost of $167,000. In the year just ended markets were found in Ontario for
806.000	tons of coal at a cost of $2,786,000. At the same time imports of coal into Ontario fell by 4,670,000 tons.
One could go on dealing with figures in this manner but, as I promised the house in the beginning, I do not want to bore the house with too many figures at this time. However, perhaps I should put this on the record. I am referring now to the report of the coal board for the year 1958-59, with the figures added in pen for the year 1959-60, the one just closed. In 1958-59 Nova Scotia coal moved under subvention amounted to 2,238,104.13 tons and the total amount of subvention paid was $8,257,741.93; in the year just closed, 1959-60, Nova Scotia coal [Mr. Nowlan.l moved under subvention amounted to 2,414,786 tons or an increase of about 175,000 tons of coal compared with the year before despite falling markets.
Look at these figures, Mr. Speaker. The opposition says, "What have you done?'' This is what the taxpayers of Canada have done under the leadership of this government and co-operating with it. Last year, 1958-59, subventions amounted to $8,257,741.93 as I said a moment ago. In the year just closed subventions provided by the government from the consolidated revenue fund of Canada on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada amounted to $13,518,396.11, and the same subvention has been provided in the estimates for the year on which we have now entered.
It is due to measures such as these that we have been able to give to the coal industry the degree of support which we have, a degree of support that I am sure is a surprise to the corporation, a surprise to the union and employees, and a very pleasant one indeed. At this juncture I think it is only fair to say that we cannot help but be impressed with the degree of co-operation of the union and the men working in these coal mines who have carried on their employment without seeking increases in pay. As a matter of fact, the corporation, the union, this government, and the government of Nova Scotia to the extent to which it has contributed, have been working together as a team and as a result of that team play the industry has been kept in this relatively strong position.
That is the present. Of the future what can one say? The future certainly is not one to cause great joy. The coal industry is facing increasing competition and undoubtedly solutions to problems will have to be found. The government, realizing that, has appointed a royal commission under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Rand to study the problems of the industry and, we hope, to come up with suggestions and solutions for at least some of its problems. Mr. Justice Rand has had a distinguished record on the bench and in the public life of the country. He has enjoyed the confidence of labour and of all the Canadian people because of his qualities of mind, his integrity and his judgment. Although no one man can accomplish miracles, I think everyone interested in the Nova Scotia coal industry is highly appreciative of the fact that the government was able to persuade Mr. Justice Rand to enter upon this task and we are very hopeful of the results which will flow from it. Those are the problems of the future.
As far as the amount of work is concerned, there will not be any greater "down time" than last year but it is expected that there

will not be as much "down time" as there was last year. The union was perfectly satisfied with the results that were achieved last year. It was not happy, of course, but very much surprised that they were as good as they were. The union representatives who were here last week met with my colleague, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois), the Prime Minister (Mr. Die-fenbaker) and myself and expressed their great appreciation of the effort that this government and the government of Nova Scotia have made in trying to cope with the problem which they admitted was one of the most serious with which any economy could be faced.
Reference was also made this afternoon by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to transportation problems, and we were somewhat chided because we had not solved all the problems set forth in the Atlantic charter. I was one of those who had something to do with the drafting of that charter and I am rather proud of it. Together with members of the House of Commons from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland I worked to draft that charter. We did not expect that we would solve all the problems in a day. We never suggested we had ready-made answers at all times to all problems. I have said enough to indicate that we have found answers to many of the problems which were confronting us when we wrote that charter. If on the afternoon and evening when we were working on the charter we could have looked forward three years and could have seen that we would have accomplished as much as we have, we would have been very pleased with ourselves indeed.
Transportation is a deep-seated problem, a deep-rooted problem, a problem of geography, a problem of history. We have a railway running in a round-about way through northern New Brunswick. It reminds one of the changes that take place in defence policy from time to time. When the British built the Rideau canal so as to be able to send troops down to the St. Lawrence it was the early D.E.W. line of Canada. In the same way, because of the danger of war with the United States, the railway was built through northern New Brunswick so as to keep it as far away as possible from the United States boundary. We are paying the price for that today with the long haul although we are assisted to some extent by the Maritime Freight Rates Act. My hon. friend spoke of the increases they made in the payments under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. That is perfectly true, but I think my hon. friend would be the first to admit that changing economic conditions, the inauguration of truck 79951-0-220

I have outlined very briefly, and very succinctly, only touching some of the highlights, what has been accomplished by this government in three years. Despite the Jeremiah wails of my friends opposite, which I suppose are natural when one is sitting in the opposition and one feels like Jeremiah that the situation is hopeless, and they undoubtedly feel more like Jeremiah than ever now, I think the greatest accomplishment is the changed outlook, the changed attitude, of the people of the maritime provinces. There is a new confidence, a new hope that was not there a few years ago.
As I have said, the problems are far from solved. However, the people today realize that they have a government in Ottawa, and governments in the provincial capitals, which are interested in their problems and are determined to find solutions in so far as solutions are possible. Despite anything that my hon. friend may, in his political enthusiasm, say about these matters, I would ask him to go back carefully over the record of his government or any other government and find accomplishments in dealing with the problems of the maritime provinces in any period of 10 years which would compare with what has been done by this government during the last three years.

The minister said it could be a mere coincidence that such an amendment was introduced at this time. I should like to tell the minister that it is not a mere coincidence, but is the result of the unemployment situation and other conditions in the Atlantic provinces. The minister referred, in a very mild manner, to what he called the political speeches made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and my colleague the hon. member for Northumberland-Mira-michi. All of us who have been in this house for a number of years know that it has not been the practice of the minister, especially when he sat on this side, to make what he would call a political speech.
The minister referred us to the grants that were paid to the Atlantic provinces. It is true that the grants which will be paid this year and which were paid- last year were bound to be higher than those that were paid in the years 1955-56 or 1956-57. We must take into consideration the increase in revenues in this country and the increase in population. I join with my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in recognizing this special grant of $25 million which is now being paid to the Atlantic provinces.
The minister referred to the coal problem in the Atlantic provinces, and particularly in Nova Scotia. He more or less intimated that we in the opposition are saying that the responsibility rests on the provincial and federal governments. I should like to say at this time that we in the opposition have not forgotten the promises made by the Conservative candidates prior to the last two federal elections, especially those from Nova Scotia. These promises were not only to maintain production and try to keep the coal mines of Cape Breton open, but to increase the production of these mines.
We have.

I question some of the
figures that were cited by the minister. The records are there to show that in the last two years the production of the coal mines of Nova Scotia has decreased by over one million tons or 25 per cent. Now, the minister may have used two specific years for comparison, but if he takes the production figures for the last two years I believe he will have to admit that the production is down by over one million tons or 25 per cent. In so far as the unions in the Cape Breton area are concerned,
I think I have enough correspondence in my 

office to show that they are not satisfied, and they are certainly not happy about what is happening in their area.
I should like now to say a few words about the Atlantic charter. The minister stated that he had taken part in the framing of this Atlantic charter. I have here in front of me the Atlantic charter. The minister said that this government had found an answer to many of the problems. Earlier in his speech, before the dinner recess, he stated that most of the problems mentioned in the Atlantic charter had been taken care of by this government. I should like to know-
I think I said an approach had been made to taking care of them. I do not believe I said they had all been taken care of.
Did I hear the minister say an approach had been made?
I said that approaches had been made to the solution of many of them. I did not say that they had been solved.

There is quite a difference between an approach to a problem and the solution of a problem. What we in the mari-times are interested in right now is the solution of the problems which are facing us. It is the implementation of what is mentioned in the Atlantic resolutions in which we are interested.
What is mentioned in the Atlantic resolutions? I have here a copy of these Atlantic resolutions, with pictures of the candidates in the province of New Brunswick. I know this is the same as the charter which was approved by the Conservative candidates in Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island. As was said this afternoon, this resolution says:
we are resolved to stand together in support of these measures which will help to overcome the historic disabilities which have limited, and even denied, opportunity to this area.
Resolution No. 1 is:
National resources development program.
Here is what it says:
We emphatically endorse John Diefenbaker's policy calling for a national development program;-
Well, I would ask the minister, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and other members from the Atlantic provinces, what has been done to endorse the policy of John Diefenbaker calling for a national development program? What has been done to develop the economy of the Atlantic provinces?

No. 2 reads:
Decentralization of industry
By united and resolute representation from the members of parliament from the Atlantic provinces, we believe that all Canadians will support a federal program of industrial decentralization.
We will urge that: 1. The Atlantic provinces receive a more equitable share of defence contract expenditures.
I should like the hon. member on the government side to produce the figures on that particular item.
2.	That crown corporations be established in the area.
I should like to have named any crown corporations that have been established in the Atlantic provinces since June of 1957.
3.	That special fiscal consideration be given to private enterprises which will encourage the location of industry in the Atlantic area and, further, encourage the processing of our natural resources here.
Here again I should like to know what special fiscal consideration has been given to industries in the Atlantic area. The answer would be absolutely none. No. 3 is:
Capital projects program
We favour the immediate institution of an Atlantic capital projects program which will provide federal capital assistance for provincial projects designed to enlarge the basic economy of the area.
But the facts are-and I will come back to this matter latter-that since this government has taken office, no capital projects of any nature have been introduced in the Atlantic provinces. No. 4 is:
Atlantic provinces power development.
Here I will admit that a bill has been passed having to do with Atlantic provinces power development. I am sure this point will be dealt with in detail by other members on this side of the house before this debate is over. No. 5 is:
Fiscal needs of the Atlantic provinces.
On this point I would say that I agree with my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who recognized the fact that additional grants are being paid to the Atlantic provinces in the amount of $25 million a year. No. 6 is:
Canadian Coastguard
We will press for a Canadian coastguard.
They have been pressing and we are still waiting for the coastguard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, the editorial I read this afternoon distinctly stated "the late 1950's".

The hon. member referred to the loan for Beechwood. What did New Brunswick really get in this loan from the federal government to finance the Beechwood project? It is true that the loan of $29,500,000 was made to the province of New Brunswick at a rate of interest of 3.78 per cent. However, at the time the bill was introduced I remember objecting in this house to the fact that the loan was granted for too short a period, namely for eight years only. The facts today show that I was right in objecting to that term of the loan. Only a few months ago the province of New Brunswick was obliged to issue bonds in New York, in the United States, where they are paying close to C per cent interest. What for? They are doing it in order to pay back to the federal government the payment of $4,358,983.39 a year which they are bound to pay according to the terms of this loan.
The facts are that the province of New Brunswick would have been better off if in 1956 or early 1957 they had gone ahead on their own and issued 40-year bonds at the current rate of interest which was then in the vicinity of 4.25 per cent or 4.50 per cent and had financed the project on their own in preference to financing it on the terms of the loan made by the federal government. That is the case of Beechwood.

Reference has been made this afternoon to Camp Gagetown in the Fredericton area. If conditions have picked up in the Saint John and Fredericton areas it is owing mainly to the construction of Camp Gagetown which was built under the previous administration.
References have also been made to the proposed Prince Edward Island causeway. I know that this was an extremely important project prior to the provincial election in Prince Edward Island last year, just as the Chignecto canal is extremely important now prior to a provincial election in New Brunswick this year. We all know that in the
1958-	59 estimates there was a sum of $360,000 for a survey for the Prince Edward Island causeway. An election was coming in Prince Edward Island in the following year. In the
1959-	60 estimates there was a sum of $250,000. This year, now that the election is over, this amount has been reduced to $50,000.
We know that the Conservative government is now in power in Prince Edward Island, and this government has been called the causeway party. But after the election was won on the island, what did we hear? We heard from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) a statement giving the objections to the construction of the causeway. They were objections which did not exist prior to the September 1 election last year on the island. What were his objections? They were that the cost was much higher than he expected; that the tide was much Stronger than anticipated; that the ice was much thicker than he had ever thought; and that it would affect movement of fish through the Northumberland strait. Those were objections which we all knew were there prior to the provincial election. But now that the election is over, now that the causeway cause has worked well, the minister can come out and give these objections.
What do we see now? We see the kind of shemozzle there is between the premier of Prince Edward Island and Premier Flemming of New Brunswick, each wondering which should get priority, whether it would be the causeway or whether it would be the Chignecto canal. However, we can be sure that, owing to the fact that the election is over, the Chignecto canal will likely get priority.


I would like to deal with the amendment which was introduced this afternoon by my colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. We recall that in "The Nation's Business" T.V. series on Wednesday, March 2, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said:
The responsibility of the federal government extends to every part of Canada. We believe in the development of Canadian resources for the benefit of all Canadians and the processing of more and more of these resources in Canada. We shall never be satisfied to see one part of the country develop and another lag behind.
I hope that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) will not be all upset and scandalized if I try to picture some of the conditions which do exist in our own province of New Brunswick today. The Prime Minister was right, he may even have been sincere, in saying "We shall never be satisfied to see one part of the country develop and another lag behind." But the question today is the following: What has the present administration done to take care of regional problems, to solve or remove the inequalities of opportunities for Canadians living in the Atlantic provinces? What has the present administration done to implement in full, or even in part, the promises, the solemn pledge, made by the Conservative candidates prior to the 1957 election? The people of the Atlantic provinces were given, as was mentioned just a few minutes ago by the Minister of National Revenue, great hope for the future development of our area by those Atlantic resolutions which were dealt with in detail by the speakers who have preceded me in this debate and to which I referred a few months ago.
The failure of the present government to implement its election promises is clearly shown not only by its omissions in its policy toward the Atlantic provinces but also by its disregard to adopt a national development policy which would ensure and preserve for the Canadian people and future generations of Canadians the control of economic destiny.
I have here a pamphlet which outlines the highlights of Progressive Conservative policy which was published by the Progressive Conservative party of Canada prior to the June 1957 election. On pages 4 and 5 are outlined the five points of the new national policy which would ensure national development, as it says, for the benefit of all. The first paragraph reads as follows:
National development. To assure economic development in all parts of this country the Conservative party will offer a new national policy founded on a renewed sense of national purpose.

Now that is very clear-"a new national policy founded on a renewed sense of national purpose". It goes on:
Whereas Sir John Macdonald was concerned with opening the west, we shall be concerned with the developments in the northern frontier.
How can we reconcile this statement of the national policy of the Conservative party with the Atlantic charter, which reads:
We emphatically endorse John Diefenbaker's policy calling for a national development program.
There is quite a difference between the program for the Atlantic provinces and the national program of the Conservative party where the Atlantic provinces are not even mentioned.
Further on in the pamphlet are stated the five points of the Conservative policy which reads as follows:
A P-C government will
1.	Adopt a national development policy in co-operation with the provinces which will develop our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, anyone would support such a policy, but we all know that this policy has not been implemented by the actions of the present government.
2.	Encourage more processing of Canada's resources in Canada.
What has this government done to encourage the processing of Canada's resources in Canada? In my own constituency of Gloucester where we have huge deposits of zinc and lead which have been dormant since March 31, 1958, a day which is familiar to hon. members on the government side, an announcement was made a few weeks ago that those minerals will be transported to Belgium in order to be processed, to be smelted. I wonder if this is to encourage the development of our natural resources in Canada.
3.	Correct the present unfavourable trade balances.
I do not have to elaborate on that because we know what the unfavourable trade balance has been in the last two years, over $1.5 billion.
4.	Foster wider financial participation by Canadians in the development of our resources.
Here again we know that the actions of the present government in this instance are almost negligible.
5.	Promote greater opportunity and employment for a steadily increasing population.
If I were discussing the unemployment situation in detail at this time I know I would be called to order, but we must all admit that now, even after the snow has gone and after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his budget speech said that unemployment
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces would go with the snow, the snow is gone and unemployment is still at an all-time high in this country.
What is the economic position of the Atlantic provinces after three years of Conservative government in Ottawa? I regret that on this point I cannot agree with the Minister of National Revenue. Where are the improvements promised by the present Prime Minister and by the Conservative candidates as outlined in their Atlantic resolutions? What is the situation in my own province of New Brunswick?
We all know that the number of manufacturing establishments in New Brunswick, which had risen from 889 in 1945 to 1,077 in 1952 had decreased to 975 in 1958 after six years of Tory administration in our own province. We know that notwithstanding the promises made by the present government the number of registrations for jobs in the Atlantic region now exceeds 125,000. In my own constituency of Gloucester over 40 per cent of the labour force is today without a job and a large number of those unemployed have exhausted their unemployment insurance stamps and are without unemployment insurance benefits.
As long as I am Prime Minister, this government will not rest while one Canadian remains out of work. No one will be allowed to suffer.
Those are the well-known words of the Prime Minister. I would ask through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Right Hon. Prime Minister, what about those 840,000 Canadians today seeking jobs, a number of them suffering from hunger and privation? In my own constituency of Gloucester I know of hundreds of children who have to attend school without proper food and in many cases without adequate clothing.
Do they pay family allowances there?

Yes, they do pay family allowances and if it were not for those family allowances and other social securities introduced by the Liberal administration those poor children would be starving today. I would ask the Prime Minister to come into my province, in my constituency of Gloucester, to come up to Sormany, Val Doucet, St. Sauveur and many other villages in my constituency, and see the misery and hardship which exists today after three years of Conservative administration. If it were not for social security benefits those poor children would be starving to death.
I do not share the views of some hon. members on the government side who take some satisfaction from the fact that such

You are rejoicing about it.

No. I am one who views with great fear and anxiety the perilous state of the unemployment insurance fund. The sum of $917 million to the credit of the fund when the present government took over had shrunk to $359 million on March 31 and will be in the vicinity of $300 million or less by the end of May this year. This decline took place in spite of the 30 per cent increase in contributions which has now been in effect for the last eight months.
, With seasonal unemployment at such a high level how can the government justify its present advertising policy abroad which was referred to in this house a few weeks ago? How can the government justify its advertising such as appeared in the Belfast Telegraph of December 6, 1959? An advertisement in that newspaper read:
Share in Canada's great future-
Immediate opportunities-
Assisted passage loans (interest free) can be arranged as required.
This advertisement appeared in the Belfast Telegraph December 6, 1959 at a time when there were over 800,000 unemployed in Canada. Notwithstanding this fact the government was advertising job openings in [DOT] Canada in these words:
Immediate opportunities for-
Bakers, bookkeepers, bricklayers, carpenters and joiners, cooks, farmers, farm workers, furniture upholsterers, hairdressers, motor mechanics, repair men, painters, plasterers, mechanic repairmen, salesmen and shop assistants-
-and others. If such immediate opportunities are available the maritime papers, I am convinced, would offer free advertising space for such jobs as I have just referred to. If the government would put the same ad in the Atlantic provinces newspapers I know that it would get all the bricklayers, carpenters and other skilled workers it needs right here in Canada.
I recently received a letter from one of my own constituents in which he asked if I could lend him $50 so he could go to Seven Islands and get a job. I did not have $50 to lend him but if I had been convinced that he had a job to go to I would have gladly borrowed the money and loaned it to him so he could have found work. The government is prepared to make interest-free loans to assist in the passage of immigrants to Canada. Why does the government not offer the same thing in Canada? Why does the government not offer to pay the passage or transportation costs of workers to areas where employment is available in Canada?


If the time has come for a change in the human outlook to improve the world we live in, the time has also come for the redeployment of some part of the huge defence expenditure this country has been called upon to undertake in order to maintain its enviable position as one of the leading nations of the world. I ask the government what steps or new measures have been introduced to take care of eventual reductions in defence expenditures, particularly as they may affect the Atlantic provinces? Reference was made to that this afternoon. Has not this government learned from its experience with the Arrow? Has it not taken a lesson from its failure to act in connection with the situation at Elliot Lake? Is not the government ashamed of its failure to provide adequate assistance to the population of Springhill following the unfortunate calamity of October, 1958? The people of Spring-hill deserved much more than the establishment in the area of a penal institution.
This government has in mind the reduction of defence expenditures. Again I ask the members of this government, particularly the four cabinet ministers from the Atlantic provinces-three with responsibility and one without responsibility-what will happen to the city of Halifax when defence establishments curtail their operations? Again I ask what provisions are being made by this government to rectify the disparity which exists in the Atlantic area and which the Atlantic resolutions, it was promised, would help?
This is the time to establish a capital projects commission as we in the opposition have been suggesting for some time. The people of the Atlantic provinces are fed up with promises, fed up with hope and vision. What they want is action and they want it now and not tomorrow. A capital projects commission for the Atlantic provinces, we know, will not suffice in itself. It must be supplemented by a tax incentive program similar to the measures introduced in England and in Belgium where they are being used to attract industries to areas hard hit by the closing of existing industries.
How can this government and the Prime Minister justify their position toward the Atlantic provinces when, at a time of unprecedented unemployment, public works projects are being drastically reduced as so obviously shown by the estimates for the current fiscal year? As I said in this house only a few weeks ago, the estimates for harbour improvements alone are cut by $3 million in Nova Scotia and by $2.5 million in New Brunswick. What major capital project was initiated in the Atlantic provinces since this government took office two years ago? Where is the $1,800 million public works program

that was supposed to take care of the unemployment situation? It has remained in the vision stage and our unemployed are given the hope-yes, the hope-of better days to come, the hope that some day, the sooner the better, a Liberal government will again take over the administration of the affairs of this country.
The people of the Atlantic provinces have not forgotten the Atlantic resolutions. They were given the hope of better times and more employment. What did they get? The highest unemployment rate on record.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) said this afternoon that the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate went further than the Atlantic resolutions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, no.

I ask hon. members on the government side from the Atlantic provinces how they can vote against a motion that calls for the establishment of an Atlantic capital projects program for the purpose of assuring the financing of projects essential to the economic development of the Atlantic provinces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the hon. member has included everything in that amendment except the kitchen sink.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has just confirmed what I mentioned his having said this afternoon. I challenge every hon. member on the government side and particularly those from the Atlantic provinces to vote against the second point in our amendment which calls for:
The provision of special fiscal incentives to private enterprise for the purpose of encouraging industrial growth and the processing of natural resources in the Atlantic provinces.
I challenge them to vote against the third point of our amendment which reads as follows:
The institution of an immediate inquiry to determine the effects of national monetary, fiscal and economic policies on the development of the Atlantic provinces and to make recommendations on desirable changes in the application of such policies for the benefit of the Atlantic provinces.
Before voting against this part of the amendment, I invite hon. members opposite to contact Premier Stanfield and Premier Flemming of New Brunswick. Here is point No. 4 of our amendment:
The adjustment of freight rates and the provision of transportation facilities to overcome the handicaps of the geographic position of the Atlantic provinces.
We had in our amendment, Mr. Speaker, the four points which are mentioned almost word
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces for word in the Atlantic charter, and the basis used by the present members of the government from the Atlantic provinces in their plea to the electors of their respective constituencies before the general election. I ask again, Mr. Speaker, can they vote against such an amendment?
In concluding my remarks I would suggest that a new APEC be formed. We know of the good work which has been done by the Atlantic provinces economic council; but if this government cannot find a solution for the Atlantic provinces, then I would suggest that an Atlantic provinces economic commission be appointed, having on its membership the members of the present Atlantic provinces economic council, representatives of the provincial governments, representatives of the different municipalities and federal officials. Such a commission, be it a royal commission if the government so desires, could make straightforward recommendations to the government which it would have to follow. Such a request of the Atlantic provinces cannot be denied.
We are not asking for hand-outs. The central provinces and the western provinces know what we of the Atlantic provinces need. Just a week ago I was visiting one of my constituents and I noticed that the car at his door was manufactured in Ontario. When I opened the door I noticed that the door knob came from Peterborough. When I walked into his house I saw that the carpet came from Ontario, the furniture came from Quebec. When I went into his kitchen I saw that the washing machine, the refrigerator, the toaster and everything were manufactured in Quebec or Ontario.
How about the lawnmower?

The lawnmower was certainly not fabricated in the Atlantic provinces. The cereals came from western Canada. Even the meat came not from the Atlantic provinces but from some of the other provinces.
In the Atlantic provinces we have an outlet of 1.5 million people to offer to the central provinces. We are an outlet for the central provinces. When we ask to be considered we know that we have to pay additional freight rates in order to get those goods. In return, what do the central provinces buy from us? Our pulp and paper are exported to the United States. Seventy five per cent to 80 per cent of our fish production is exported to the United States or to South America.
I again emphasize the fact that we are not asking for hand-outs; we are just asking for the rights of the people of the Atlantic provinces.

What have you done?

I have long since stopped looking for gems from that corner of the house.
I looked up the Canadian Parliamentary Guide during the supper recess to find out some of the antecedents, the genealogy of this self-appointed champion of the Atlantic provinces; born in Ontario,-

Mr. Speaker, with the greatest possible reluctance I raise a question of privilege. I was elected by my constituents on three occasions.
