Hear, hear.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
You cannot make a silk purse out of a sow's ear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would ask the hon. member for Halifax to come back to the subject matter.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to raise a point of order. Since the hon. member for Halifax has lectured us on parliamentary procedure, I do raise a point of order seriously. I have examined carefully the C.C.F. subamendment as well as the amendment I moved and I find nothing in them that has anything to do with my career before I came into the house. Interesting though it is-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Your qualifications are very interesting.

-and flattered though I am to have all this attention bestowed upon me, I think it would be more in keeping with the rules of the house if the hon. gentleman would not seek so obviously to evade debating this important resolution which sets out the Tory policy on which he was elected.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if hon. gentlemen opposite will contain themselves long enough I will get to the subject matter of the amendment. We have had a remarkable performance in the provincial campaign field from gentlemen who make a habit of ridiculing us on this side about the vision and whose own vision is limited by the green carpeting down the centre of two legislative assemblies, one in Fredericton and one in Halifax. That is the vision of their party.
I have a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the hon. member how he would know what an hon. gentleman would be like.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's friends in the house on that side were making such a noise in their enthusiasm for his interesting interjection that I could not possibly hear it.
No, you would not answer it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
We have had today a further demonstration of the self-dictated piety of opposition members about the Atlantic resolutions. This is a carefully nurtured propagandist weapon in connection with which they always say before mentioning these resolutions, "Of course, Conservative members will not mind repetition of these Atlantic resolutions". This is intended to inculcate among unsuspecting people of the country the idea that we have something to be ashamed of. Let this be perfectly clear. The Atlantic resolutions to which I signed my name-I notice that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate smiles but I find this a very serious subject-were in my view the most high-minded statement of public purpose by
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces devoted young men in contemporary Canadian political history. The resolutions were and are and will remain a beacon of light after 20 years of darkness for the people of the Atlantic provinces.
I have said before, and will say as long as the electorate and breath allow me, that the Liberal party is doing the Atlantic provinces great harm by insolently repeating over and over again the most depressingly black picture which they can manage to portray of the Atlantic provinces. What are the facts?
Unemployment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: In the publication, Private and Public Investment in Canada, Outlook for 1960, Regional Investment, issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, the investment intentions of the province of Nova Scotia are given as these. Total investment intentions of primary industry and the construction industry, manufacturing, utilities, trade, finance and commercial services, housing, institutional services and government departments are given as $184.2 million in 1958, $205,800,000 in 1959 and $219,500,000 in 1960. What is backward about that?
Good intentions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
If you go forward the opposition says you are going backwards. The total of all capital and repair expenditures in 1958 was $258,400,000, in 1959, $284 million and in 1960, $299.5 million. We have here the highest capital intentions of any year in Nova Scotia's history, which betokens the degree of optimistic faith our people have in the province of Nova Scotia.
I am sure that the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, who introduced the amendment, will not say that I am out of order if I mention his beautiful constituency, the entrance to Notre Dame bay and the port of Twillingate. In listening to him this afternoon. I thought that the way you get into Twillingate is between two dangerous headlands. One is called Hell's gate and the other is called Paradise and down the middle is Twillingate. We have to be very careful going down the middle of the remarks which we heard this afternoon.
Let us contrast the health and welfare programs in Nova Scotia with those of the last year of Liberal rule, 1956. The province now pays the cost of the care of all tubercular mentally ill people. Because of federal financial assistance the province is able to pay one third of the operating cost of municipal hospitals for the mentally ill which meet the minimum and desirable standards of professional practice. The province has now agreed to raise its share of these costs to one half. In 1956 the Liberal government

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces paid nothing. Already half of the mentally ill under municipal care are in hospitals which have qualified for provincial assistance.
The province is able now, because of its financial situation, to supply helpful new drugs to municipal institutions. Psychiatric clinics have been opened. They had to be opened. More people became mentally ill under the Liberal government than ever before in our history. Over $3 million has been spent to improve the Nova Scotia hospital. A new nurses' residence is to be built. The hospital plan has been instituted and outpatients' service has already been expanded.
There is a shortage of hospital beds in Nova Scotia today because in the years from 1951 to 1956 the Liberal government of Nova Scotia discontinued matching federal grants for new hospital bed construction. The consequence was that nothing could be given, and that brought new hospital construction virtually to a halt. One of the first things the government of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker did on assuming office was to increase the federal grant to $2,000, and the Stanfield government put up an extra $3,000, so that the Conservatives, who we are told have no regard for the average human being, made possible grants of $5,000 for every new hospital bed in Nova Scotia.
But hon. gentlemen will recall that as early as 1919 the government of Mackenzie King promised hospital insurance in this country, and yet 37 years later a Liberal government in Nova Scotia was not paying anything for new hospital beds.
Shame.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: We now have an extension to the Halifax infirmary because of the zeal and vision of the Sisters of Charity. A $8 million treatment centre is being planned for the Victoria general hospital, a provincial institution. A contract has been let for a new hospital at Yarmouth. In Nova Scotia, the local Liberals tried to diminish the fact that the provincial government concluded an agreement for a chemical pulpmill on the strait of Canso costing $40 million. The Liberal members say, "We wanted the pulp-mill, but we did not want them to take any land on which to build it."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; I must say that the hon. member is worrying me with his remarks now. I think he is straying a little too far from the motion before the house. The terms of the motion are very wide indeed, but I think there has to be a relationship between his remarks and federal policies or federal administration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
I, of course, bow immediately to your ruling. I was tempted to cite those

things because the last gentleman who spoke dwelt at great length on his own constituency. At least I am talking about provincial government. However, if the rules are such that I must refer to federal activities, let me refer to the federal activities in my own riding which has been mentioned. I noticed a great deal of concern about Halifax in the house today. For instance, there was the repetitious Liberal argument, how will disarmament affect Halifax? One wonders whether this party, devoted to peace, is interested in disarmament as a means of contributing to the spiritual development of man or as a means of trying to embarrass the Conservatives. I am not afraid of disarmament, not in Halifax or anywhere in the world.
Let us look at what has taken place in a replica area of the maritime provinces under this government. In the city of Halifax we are completing a $4.5 million addition to the Nova Scotian hotel, promised by the Liberals for 20 years. We bailed out the bankrupt contractor of the former Liberal administration and completed the Ralston building. We have nearly completed a $1.5 million Bank of Canada agency building. Tenders have been called for a major addition to the federal building in Halifax. Work is already under way on a quarter of a million dollar addition to the federal building at Dartmouth. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois), who is sometimes asked, what are you doing for the maritime provinces, has helped us to secure a $6 million oceanographic research station near Halifax. Tenders have been called for the approaches and for the piers and jetties for that great institute.
There has been an investment of $4.5 million in the Mulgrave park housing development; that construction job is already under way and will shortly be joined by another public housing development. A $16 million federal investment, commenced by the former administration and added to and improved by this administration for the Halifax international airport, is shortly to come to fruition with operational flying to commence on July 14. We have put up numerous new buildings in defence installations such as H.M.C. Dockyard, Shearwater, Beaver Bank, and a naval armament depot. The Fairey Aviation Company, one month ago, had the highest employment in its history at Eastern passage, largely because of the federal government's procurement practices. The Halifax shipyard in recent months has incurred the same fate as shipyards throughout the world. However, it now faces a period in which re-employment will take place as a new destroyer

escort and a new Department of Transport ferry will be in the slips for construction. We now have four new industries in the industrial estates park at Woodside.
Not all of our people are employed. The hon. gentleman who preceded me talked about a reduction in the amount of money for harbours and rivers. There are 86 fishermen's wharves, public wharves, in my constituency, and 59 of these have had to be repaired in the last three years. Some of these were in despicable shape. As recently as this morning we had to call tenders to remove the outside end of one at Sheet Harbour where the Liberals had helpfully taken out the crib which lay between the outside end and the shore. How can fishermen use a wharf which is wharf here, the open water, and then shore line? I suppose it was built by one of their friends.
If the rules of the house, Mr. Speaker, had been interpreted more generously I might have had an opportunity to refer here to some remarks made about Liberal leaders in the Atlantic provinces. Mr. Hicks says that he would like to come up here and have a heart to heart, man to man talk with Mr. Diefenbaker. The man with whom he should have had the heart to heart talk was Louis St. Laurent, or is it possible that he did?
The present federal administration pays the province of Nova Scotia over $10 million more than did the previous Liberal government. I walked into this house tonight, as one of the two members for Halifax, to say how grateful my people are for the fact that this new money is coming into my riding and into the ridings of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse) and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Legere), and all the other great constituencies in Nova Scotia. These additional federal moneys have made possible new schools, new roads, new housing and a new life of hope for our people.
I want to say this: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has had a little less than seven years of durability in the Atlantic provinces. The rest of us in the Atlantic area do not always regard age as synonymous with wisdom, but it is certainly a good primary basis. Some of us have been there a few years longer. Perhaps the hon. gentleman has not been a resident of Newfoundland long enough to know some of the delightful phrases. One of them that I like, for obvious reasons, is a saying they have in Newfoundland, "It is not every day that Morris kills a cow". This means to say that it is not every day that you get an opportunity to tell what
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces is in your heart, and when you get it, tell it. There is another classic one, "Your tauts are too far aft". The word "taut" is Newfoundland for the word "thwart". It means the cross seat in the boat. When your tauts are too far aft, it means you are so mixed up that your opinions are not worth listening to.

I had an
opportunity to listen to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris) for only a short while, Mr. Speaker, but what little I heard convinced me that his thwart is far too far aft. He asked for that. He chose the simile himself. If I were in the boat with my hon. friend, I think I would keep him as far aft as possible. In fact, I think I would put him overboard and tow him along.
I rose to support the amendment made by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). I think it was Lincoln who said that no nation can survive half slave and half free. I believe that statement is true in an economic sense as well. The problem of the Atlantic provinces is not a regional one; it is a national one. Just as no nation can exist half slave and half free, so also a nation like Canada cannot exist if one region is condemned to be permanently hewers of wood and drawers of water for another part. Canada belongs to all Canadians. Every Canadian, no matter in what part of Canada he lives, is entitled first of all to equality of opportunity and, second, to the enjoyment of a minimum level of public services.
The problem of the Atlantic provinces has not come about as a result of an economic accident. The position in which the Atlantic provinces find themselves today can be traced directly to three main causes. In the first place, it is a direct result of the step the maritime provinces or rather-I think I can include Newfoundland and say this-the Atlantic provinces took when they joined with the central provinces to make the nation of Canada.
In the second place, it is the result of the failure of the central provinces to live up to their part of the bargain; their part of the conditions undertaken; or their part of the terms of the union.
In the third place, it is the result of federal policies which have been developed since confederation mainly to suit the economic conditions of the central provinces. If the maritime provinces had chosen not to join with the central provinces but to federate among themselves and to form a sort of Atlantic union and if they had survived as a political and geographic unit, as I think was quite probable, there is no doubt that today they would be far better off

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces than they are at the present time and that they could very well be as prosperous as other parts of Canada.
Prior to confederation the Atlantic provinces were far better off than were the central provinces. They had lower taxes. They had very small provincial debts. Their prosperity was due mainly to their own enterprise and initiative but also to the external trade which was a natural development of their position on the Atlantic seaboard. Their very low tariffs enabled them to trade in the world markets and to sell their own products, to carry them in their own bottoms to all parts of the world and to buy necessities from other countries at the lowest cost. That sort of situation encouraged the shipping industry and it was the shipping industry which produced the greatest revenue to the maritime provinces. The shipping industry, of course, is allied with the shipbuilding industry and that afforded them on outlet by means of which to utilize their forests and skills in shipbuilding and their skills which they developed in managing and sailing ships to every part of the world. They were able to turn all this to very good account financially.
There was great scope for the small enterpriser who was not hampered too much with tight money and who was free to produce any product he could sell. He knew that he could produce it at a low cost, that he could sell it at a low cost and that he could usually find a very good market for it.
When they joined up with the central provinces to form Canada the maritime provinces lost those great advantages. Instead of their own tariffs which could be suited to their own particular needs and to the needs of their own particular industries they became the victims of tariffs which were set up mainly for the protection of industry in the central provinces.
In other words, they became a captive market to the central provinces and that is the very identical situation in which Newfoundland finds itself today. Under that situation when they were forced to buy in the domestic market it was natural that the external trade, their great source of prosperity, would decline, and along with that decline in trade there must of necessity come a decline in the shipping industry and in the shipbuilding industry.
Part of the inducement held out to the maritimes to join with the central provinces was that they would ship their products through maritime ports, but after confederation this did not happen. The central provinces still continued to ship their goods through the United States ports of Boston


and New York. They did not ship to Halifax and Saint John as had been promised. The great emporiums and manufacturing centres which had been envisioned as springing up on the sea coast of the Atlantic provinces did not materialize. At that time they had thought that as the result of confederation the maritime ports would gradually take on the same function as the United States ports in the state of Maine and the state of Massachusetts which had become the manufacturing centres for the hinterland. But this did not happen. The promised railway which was to link them up with Montreal was ten years in coming, and when it did come, as the hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) pointed out this evening, it was built for military purposes and followed a route determined by military requirements rather than by economic considerations.
As a result of all this, maritime industries have been handicapped by excessive transportation costs, and instead of being the most prosperous part of Canada they have now become something akin to the poorhouse of Canada. In late years they have found themselves in the position of having to accept handouts in various forms, like tax rentals, stabilization grants, subventions and other forms of payments.
Who started the tax rentals?

I am not worrying about who started them, I am referring to them as a condition resulting from the failure to live up to the obligations undertaken which were accepted at the time they became part of Canada.
Now although they have suffered those handicaps they have still seen their taxes used to build great national projects like the St. Lawrence seaway, which will be of great benefit to the central provinces but has not proved to date to be of any great benefit to the maritimes. We hope that the time will come when that condition will change, but experience to date has not tended to give very much encouragement.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) paid great tribute this afternoon to the contributions which the people of the maritimes have made to the development of the rest of Canada. In fact, without the maritimes there could never have been any Canadian nation. The central provinces were too vulnerable to exist by themselves and would certainly have become a part of the United States economy many years ago. Since then the maritime provinces have for many years been bearing almost alone the full cost of making Canada a nation and enabling Canada to exist as a nation. That cost should not be shared by the maritime

provinces alone. It is cost that properly belongs to all Canadians and to all parts of Canada.
Therefore the payments which have been made to the Atlantic provinces should be viewed in that light, not as handouts or as generous gifts but as a national obligation. In fact, I think one could almost use the word restitution.
We cannot begin to cure the ills of the Atlantic provinces without understanding the causes and either removing them or offsetting their effect. The Atlantic charter-I mean the political one in 1957, not the historic Atlantic charter-was merely a statement of goals. But what is needed is a planned policy to implement these goals, such as some sort of five-year or three-year program or some other fixed period of priorities and progressive development.
Business of the House
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

Before you leave the chair, sir, I wonder if the house leader could give us some idea of the business for Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, if it is at all possible, for convenience in arranging for speakers in debate.
